Title: Monument of the Discoveries - Portugal
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
Site:Padrão dos Descobrimentos, Portugal Student/Author:Chaney Fix ’26

## Background
The Monument of the Discoveries, or Padrão dos Descobrimentos, stands 170 feet tall along the picturesque bank of the Tagus River in Lisbon, Portugal. Located in the Santa Maria de Belém area, the site commemorates prominent historical figures from the 15th and 16th century Portuguese Age of Discovery. The monument was originally constructed for the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition as a temporary exhibit to celebrate Portugal’s maritime prowess and national pride. Originally constructed out of perishable materials, the statue was reconstructed in 1960 in honor of the fifth centenary of Prince Henry the Navigator, the monument’s forefront figure. The figures behind Henry represent important Portuguese leaders that succeeded Henry’s time, including monarchs, explorers, scientists, and missionaries. Some of the most renowned include Vasco de Gama, Pedro Álvares Cabral, and Ferdinand Magellan. The monument was rebuilt using cement and rose-colored stone, with limestone figures.
The design of the structure is meant to invoke the prow of a caravel, a Portuguese sailing ship instrumental during Portuguese exploration, while the entrance resembles a sword, a symbol of the Portuguese military and strength. In front of the monument sits an enormous pavement featuring a map of Portuguese voyages, crafted in traditional Portuguese patterns of multi-colored limestone and marble. This map serves as a visual representation of Portugal’s extensive maritime explorations and conquests. It can be viewed best from the overlook located at the top of the monument.

## Analysis
The Monument of the Discoveries is more than a tribute, but rather a statement of Portuguese power and influence. The large figures scaling the sides of the structure, combined with the imposing sword-like entrance and caravel design, emphasize this extensive naval power. However, it is critical to remember that this power came at the expense of other nations and cultures, reflecting a complex and controversial legacy. The so-called “Age of Discovery” was a period during which the Portuguese empire came into contact with other nations, frequently leading to their colonization. While the monument remains a powerful symbol of Portugal’s historical impact on global exploration, it should additionally prompt reflection on the broader consequences of imperialism and push modern-day Portugal to further reparations.
Today, the site is visited by large numbers of tourists throughout the year due to its grandiose appearance and placement between the historic Belém Tower and Jerónimos Monastery. Most visitors pay the entrance fee thinking that their tour will solely consist of a laborious climb up a few floors for a nice view of Belem, Lisbon, but they would be dismissing the museum on the bottom floor. While one might expect this museum to detail the history of the monument, it is dedicated to an entirely different story.
Titled “Family Albums, Photographs of the African Diaspora in Greater Lisbon (1975 to Today),” the bottom floor of the site contains various media depicting the community of African people and people of African origin living in the Lisbon area. This gallery is temporary, implemented as a part of the United Nations’ International Decade for People of African Descent (2015–2024). In collaboration with the UN’s recognition efforts, Portuguese cultural and historical societies are also celebrating the lives of the many black Portuguese people descended from Africans who lived under Portuguese colonial rule. The exhibit includes everything from vintage family photographs to televised interviews to modern-day TikTok posts by black Portuguese creators. Each piece of media is accompanied by a brief story, shared by the featured individuals or their family and friends. Despite the important contents of this exhibit, there is little to no promotional material outside or on the ground floor of the monument and thus the onus falls on museum staff to direct visitors downstairs.

## Analysis
The creation of this museum is particularly intriguing when considering its origins during the 1960s, a pivotal decade for African independence. During this period, many African nations achieved independence from European colonial powers, including 17 countries in 1960 alone. Following the end of the Portuguese Salazar regime in 1974 and the dissolution of colonial rule, Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, and Cape Verde all gained independence from Portugal by the end of 1975. This development led to a significant influx of immigrants from these former colonies to Portugal, “over one million people – that is to say, an increase in the population of over 12.5 per cent” (Marques 2012, 128).
In response to this demographic shift, “the post-revolutionary Portuguese government had made a pledge to achieve decolonization” and “to accommodate the sudden demographic outburst resulting from those who decided to settle” (Marques 2012, 130). Measures included providing welfare, emergency housing, employment, and documentation. Alongside these efforts, a broader cultural renaissance emerged, with a resurgence of previously suppressed traditions and a rise in African identity across various nations, reflecting the growth of Pan-Africanism and a sense of unity among African countries. The “Family Albums” museum celebrates this rich heritage and the identity of African people and their descendants living in Portugal today. It highlights the beauty and significance of their family heritage and traditions, honoring the legacy and continuity of their cultural contributions over time.

## Analysis
The Monument of the Discoveries remains one of the most visited sites in Portugal today and likely will remain so for many generations to come. The impressive design and scale of the site, as well as recognizable figures, inspire visitors to delve deeper into the profound impact that Portugal’s naval and military might had on global exploration during the Age of Exploration. Today, the monument attracts visitors eager to appreciate its historical significance and scenic views of Lisbon, but it also houses the “Family Albums” contemporary exhibit. This exhibit, while temporary, makes an effort to highlight the often-overlooked consequences of colonialism on other nations and cultures. This gallery shifts the focus from the past to the present while acknowledging and celebrating the rich and diverse contributions of its African communities. At the conclusion of this temporary exhibition, it can only be hoped that the monument will fill the space so that it both celebrates and critically examines Portugal’s complex history, encouraging ongoing dialogue and reflection.

## Works Cited
Marques, M. Margarida. 2012. “Postcolonial Portugal: Between Scylla and Charybdis.” In Postcolonial Migrants and Identity Politics: Europe, Russia, Japan and the United States in Comparison, edited by Ulbe Bosma, Jan Lucassen, and Gert Oostindie. Berghahn Books.

From Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Vasco da Gama Pillar  
 [Wikimedia | © OpenStreetMap](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#/map/0 "Show in full screen")  
Coordinates3°13′26″S 40°07′47″E / 3.22395°S 40.12965°E  
LocationMalindi, Kilifi County, Kenya  
Completion date 1498 or 1499
The **Vasco da Gama Pillar** in Malindi, Kenya, was erected by the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama. It was constructed in 1498 or 1499 during his pioneering expedition from Lisbon to India via the Cape of Good Hope (1497–1499).
Vasco da Gama visited Malindi from 15 to 24 April 1498. He was well received by the sultan of Malindi and was provided with food, fresh water and a pilot to take the trip across the Indian Ocean to Calicut (modern-day Kozhikode).[[1]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-1) During the voyage, the explorer was allowed to erect a pillar, which included a cross made of Portuguese limestone. Most historians suggest that this happened on his return from India in 1499.[[2]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-2) The pillar in Malindi is the only one, which erected along the coast of Africa by the Portuguese and survived in its original form.[[3]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-3)
The pillar today is Malindi's most visited heritage site. Restoration work carried out since 2020 has included repairs of the existing seawalls and the pillar itself, the construction of a access route and washrooms for visitors.[[4]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-4) Access to the pillar is subject to an entry ticket.

*   

*   

*   

*   Kenyan stamps of 1998 celebrated the quincentenary of Vasco da Gama's visit.[[5]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-5) One of the stamps showcased the pillar in an painter's impression that gave the pillar the traditional thin-column elevation rather than the conical form of the reinforced pillar and the massive cross visible today.

*   Vasco da Gama Pillar described and repeatedly mentioned in the novels _“Once in Malindi”_[[6]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-6) and _“Our Wild Sex in Malindi”_[[7]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-7) (by Andrei Gusev). The novels describe a few years living in Malindi of Russian writer Andy and his wife Jennifer, who was born in Kenya.[[8]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-9)

### Overview
Padrão dos Descobrimentos, also known as the Monument to the Discoveries, is a prominent memorial located in the Belem district of Lisbon. The monument was built in 1960 to commemorate the 500th anniversary of the death of Prince Henry the Navigator, a famous Portuguese explorer and navigator. The monument is shaped like a ship's prow and features several prominent figures from Portuguese history, including Henry the Navigator, Vasco da Gama, and Ferdinand Magellan.

### What To Expect?
There is a museum located inside that showcases Portugal's maritime history and the Age of Discoveries. The museum features interactive exhibits, artefacts, and multimedia displays that allow visitors to learn about the explorers and navigators who played a significant role in shaping Portugal's history and culture.

opened.information:
Source: https://nanovic.nd.edu/research/research-initiatives/student-research-projects/sites-of-memory-in-contemporary-europe/portugal-monument-of-the-discoveries/
Title: Monument of the Discoveries - Portugal
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
Site:Padrão dos Descobrimentos, Portugal Student/Author:Chaney Fix ’26

## Background
The Monument of the Discoveries, or Padrão dos Descobrimentos, stands 170 feet tall along the picturesque bank of the Tagus River in Lisbon, Portugal. Located in the Santa Maria de Belém area, the site commemorates prominent historical figures from the 15th and 16th century Portuguese Age of Discovery. The monument was originally constructed for the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition as a temporary exhibit to celebrate Portugal’s maritime prowess and national pride. Originally constructed out of perishable materials, the statue was reconstructed in 1960 in honor of the fifth centenary of Prince Henry the Navigator, the monument’s forefront figure. The figures behind Henry represent important Portuguese leaders that succeeded Henry’s time, including monarchs, explorers, scientists, and missionaries. Some of the most renowned include Vasco de Gama, Pedro Álvares Cabral, and Ferdinand Magellan. The monument was rebuilt using cement and rose-colored stone, with limestone figures.
The design of the structure is meant to invoke the prow of a caravel, a Portuguese sailing ship instrumental during Portuguese exploration, while the entrance resembles a sword, a symbol of the Portuguese military and strength. In front of the monument sits an enormous pavement featuring a map of Portuguese voyages, crafted in traditional Portuguese patterns of multi-colored limestone and marble. This map serves as a visual representation of Portugal’s extensive maritime explorations and conquests. It can be viewed best from the overlook located at the top of the monument.

## Analysis
The Monument of the Discoveries is more than a tribute, but rather a statement of Portuguese power and influence. The large figures scaling the sides of the structure, combined with the imposing sword-like entrance and caravel design, emphasize this extensive naval power. However, it is critical to remember that this power came at the expense of other nations and cultures, reflecting a complex and controversial legacy. The so-called “Age of Discovery” was a period during which the Portuguese empire came into contact with other nations, frequently leading to their colonization. While the monument remains a powerful symbol of Portugal’s historical impact on global exploration, it should additionally prompt reflection on the broader consequences of imperialism and push modern-day Portugal to further reparations.
Today, the site is visited by large numbers of tourists throughout the year due to its grandiose appearance and placement between the historic Belém Tower and Jerónimos Monastery. Most visitors pay the entrance fee thinking that their tour will solely consist of a laborious climb up a few floors for a nice view of Belem, Lisbon, but they would be dismissing the museum on the bottom floor. While one might expect this museum to detail the history of the monument, it is dedicated to an entirely different story.
Titled “Family Albums, Photographs of the African Diaspora in Greater Lisbon (1975 to Today),” the bottom floor of the site contains various media depicting the community of African people and people of African origin living in the Lisbon area. This gallery is temporary, implemented as a part of the United Nations’ International Decade for People of African Descent (2015–2024). In collaboration with the UN’s recognition efforts, Portuguese cultural and historical societies are also celebrating the lives of the many black Portuguese people descended from Africans who lived under Portuguese colonial rule. The exhibit includes everything from vintage family photographs to televised interviews to modern-day TikTok posts by black Portuguese creators. Each piece of media is accompanied by a brief story, shared by the featured individuals or their family and friends. Despite the important contents of this exhibit, there is little to no promotional material outside or on the ground floor of the monument and thus the onus falls on museum staff to direct visitors downstairs.

## Analysis
The creation of this museum is particularly intriguing when considering its origins during the 1960s, a pivotal decade for African independence. During this period, many African nations achieved independence from European colonial powers, including 17 countries in 1960 alone. Following the end of the Portuguese Salazar regime in 1974 and the dissolution of colonial rule, Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, and Cape Verde all gained independence from Portugal by the end of 1975. This development led to a significant influx of immigrants from these former colonies to Portugal, “over one million people – that is to say, an increase in the population of over 12.5 per cent” (Marques 2012, 128).
In response to this demographic shift, “the post-revolutionary Portuguese government had made a pledge to achieve decolonization” and “to accommodate the sudden demographic outburst resulting from those who decided to settle” (Marques 2012, 130). Measures included providing welfare, emergency housing, employment, and documentation. Alongside these efforts, a broader cultural renaissance emerged, with a resurgence of previously suppressed traditions and a rise in African identity across various nations, reflecting the growth of Pan-Africanism and a sense of unity among African countries. The “Family Albums” museum celebrates this rich heritage and the identity of African people and their descendants living in Portugal today. It highlights the beauty and significance of their family heritage and traditions, honoring the legacy and continuity of their cultural contributions over time.

## Analysis
The Monument of the Discoveries remains one of the most visited sites in Portugal today and likely will remain so for many generations to come. The impressive design and scale of the site, as well as recognizable figures, inspire visitors to delve deeper into the profound impact that Portugal’s naval and military might had on global exploration during the Age of Exploration. Today, the monument attracts visitors eager to appreciate its historical significance and scenic views of Lisbon, but it also houses the “Family Albums” contemporary exhibit. This exhibit, while temporary, makes an effort to highlight the often-overlooked consequences of colonialism on other nations and cultures. This gallery shifts the focus from the past to the present while acknowledging and celebrating the rich and diverse contributions of its African communities. At the conclusion of this temporary exhibition, it can only be hoped that the monument will fill the space so that it both celebrates and critically examines Portugal’s complex history, encouraging ongoing dialogue and reflection.

# Torre Vasco Da Gama – crow’s nest of Lissabon
**Torre Vasco da Gama** is named after one of Portugal’s most important figures in history, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama. Not only is the building named after this famous seafarer, it’s also built as a ship.

# Torre Vasco Da Gama – crow’s nest of Lissabon
## Built like a ship
The tube where the elevator is located, resembles the mast of a ship. The steel is the sail and high up in the top is a crow’s nest. Just like Vasco da Gama and his traveling companions, you can enjoy a wide and beautiful view from the crow’s nest.
Have a fear of heights? Be warned, the tower is 145 meters high! To get there you go up with a lift with panorama glass – these have been in maintenance for a long time. The glass always makes it a bit easier for me to go to great heights.
The tower has been connected to a luxury hotel for a number of years. This gives it the look of a hotel in Dubai. The tower is also accessible for non-hotel guests.
Another interesting fact: Torre Vasco da Gama is the tallest building in Lisbon.

# Torre Vasco Da Gama – crow’s nest of Lissabon
## How to get to Torre Vasco da Gama
Address: Cais das Naus, Parque das Nações
Opening hours: apr-sep Mon-Thu 10 a.m – 8 p.m. and Fri-Sun 10 a.m – 10 p.m. | Oct-Mar daily 10 a.m. – 8 p.m.

texts.1:
## Background
The Monument of the Discoveries, or Padrão dos Descobrimentos, stands 170 feet tall along the picturesque bank of the Tagus River in Lisbon, Portugal. Located in the Santa Maria de Belém area, the site commemorates prominent historical figures from the 15th and 16th century Portuguese Age of Discovery. The monument was originally constructed for the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition as a temporary exhibit to celebrate Portugal’s maritime prowess and national pride. Originally constructed out of perishable materials, the statue was reconstructed in 1960 in honor of the fifth centenary of Prince Henry the Navigator, the monument’s forefront figure. The figures behind Henry represent important Portuguese leaders that succeeded Henry’s time, including monarchs, explorers, scientists, and missionaries. Some of the most renowned include Vasco de Gama, Pedro Álvares Cabral, and Ferdinand Magellan. The monument was rebuilt using cement and rose-colored stone, with limestone figures.
The design of the structure is meant to invoke the prow of a caravel, a Portuguese sailing ship instrumental during Portuguese exploration, while the entrance resembles a sword, a symbol of the Portuguese military and strength. In front of the monument sits an enormous pavement featuring a map of Portuguese voyages, crafted in traditional Portuguese patterns of multi-colored limestone and marble. This map serves as a visual representation of Portugal’s extensive maritime explorations and conquests. It can be viewed best from the overlook located at the top of the monument.
texts.2:
## Analysis
The Monument of the Discoveries is more than a tribute, but rather a statement of Portuguese power and influence. The large figures scaling the sides of the structure, combined with the imposing sword-like entrance and caravel design, emphasize this extensive naval power. However, it is critical to remember that this power came at the expense of other nations and cultures, reflecting a complex and controversial legacy. The so-called “Age of Discovery” was a period during which the Portuguese empire came into contact with other nations, frequently leading to their colonization. While the monument remains a powerful symbol of Portugal’s historical impact on global exploration, it should additionally prompt reflection on the broader consequences of imperialism and push modern-day Portugal to further reparations.
Today, the site is visited by large numbers of tourists throughout the year due to its grandiose appearance and placement between the historic Belém Tower and Jerónimos Monastery. Most visitors pay the entrance fee thinking that their tour will solely consist of a laborious climb up a few floors for a nice view of Belem, Lisbon, but they would be dismissing the museum on the bottom floor. While one might expect this museum to detail the history of the monument, it is dedicated to an entirely different story.
Titled “Family Albums, Photographs of the African Diaspora in Greater Lisbon (1975 to Today),” the bottom floor of the site contains various media depicting the community of African people and people of African origin living in the Lisbon area. This gallery is temporary, implemented as a part of the United Nations’ International Decade for People of African Descent (2015–2024). In collaboration with the UN’s recognition efforts, Portuguese cultural and historical societies are also celebrating the lives of the many black Portuguese people descended from Africans who lived under Portuguese colonial rule. The exhibit includes everything from vintage family photographs to televised interviews to modern-day TikTok posts by black Portuguese creators. Each piece of media is accompanied by a brief story, shared by the featured individuals or their family and friends. Despite the important contents of this exhibit, there is little to no promotional material outside or on the ground floor of the monument and thus the onus falls on museum staff to direct visitors downstairs.
texts.3:
## Analysis
The creation of this museum is particularly intriguing when considering its origins during the 1960s, a pivotal decade for African independence. During this period, many African nations achieved independence from European colonial powers, including 17 countries in 1960 alone. Following the end of the Portuguese Salazar regime in 1974 and the dissolution of colonial rule, Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, and Cape Verde all gained independence from Portugal by the end of 1975. This development led to a significant influx of immigrants from these former colonies to Portugal, “over one million people – that is to say, an increase in the population of over 12.5 per cent” (Marques 2012, 128).
In response to this demographic shift, “the post-revolutionary Portuguese government had made a pledge to achieve decolonization” and “to accommodate the sudden demographic outburst resulting from those who decided to settle” (Marques 2012, 130). Measures included providing welfare, emergency housing, employment, and documentation. Alongside these efforts, a broader cultural renaissance emerged, with a resurgence of previously suppressed traditions and a rise in African identity across various nations, reflecting the growth of Pan-Africanism and a sense of unity among African countries. The “Family Albums” museum celebrates this rich heritage and the identity of African people and their descendants living in Portugal today. It highlights the beauty and significance of their family heritage and traditions, honoring the legacy and continuity of their cultural contributions over time.

The Monument of the Discoveries remains one of the most visited sites in Portugal today and likely will remain so for many generations to come. The impressive design and scale of the site, as well as recognizable figures, inspire visitors to delve deeper into the profound impact that Portugal’s naval and military might had on global exploration during the Age of Exploration. Today, the monument attracts visitors eager to appreciate its historical significance and scenic views of Lisbon, but it also houses the “Family Albums” contemporary exhibit. This exhibit, while temporary, makes an effort to highlight the often-overlooked consequences of colonialism on other nations and cultures. This gallery shifts the focus from the past to the present while acknowledging and celebrating the rich and diverse contributions of its African communities. At the conclusion of this temporary exhibition, it can only be hoped that the monument will fill the space so that it both celebrates and critically examines Portugal’s complex history, encouraging ongoing dialogue and reflection.

From Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Vasco da Gama Pillar  
 [Wikimedia | © OpenStreetMap](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#/map/0 "Show in full screen")  
Coordinates3°13′26″S 40°07′47″E / 3.22395°S 40.12965°E  
LocationMalindi, Kilifi County, Kenya  
Completion date 1498 or 1499
The **Vasco da Gama Pillar** in Malindi, Kenya, was erected by the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama. It was constructed in 1498 or 1499 during his pioneering expedition from Lisbon to India via the Cape of Good Hope (1497–1499).
Vasco da Gama visited Malindi from 15 to 24 April 1498. He was well received by the sultan of Malindi and was provided with food, fresh water and a pilot to take the trip across the Indian Ocean to Calicut (modern-day Kozhikode).[[1]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-1) During the voyage, the explorer was allowed to erect a pillar, which included a cross made of Portuguese limestone. Most historians suggest that this happened on his return from India in 1499.[[2]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-2) The pillar in Malindi is the only one, which erected along the coast of Africa by the Portuguese and survived in its original form.[[3]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-3)
The pillar today is Malindi's most visited heritage site. Restoration work carried out since 2020 has included repairs of the existing seawalls and the pillar itself, the construction of a access route and washrooms for visitors.[[4]](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_Pillar#cite_note-4) Access to the pillar is subject to an entry ticket.

Title: Malindi Museum – National Museums of Kenya
Chunks: 0
**The Vasco Da Gama Pillar**
The 15th Century was an era of worldwide exploration by Portugal. Early in the Century, Portugal had conceived an idea of commemorating visits of Portuguese vessels in different domains. In 1497, King Dom Manuel of Portugal appointed Vasco da Gama to command a fleet of 4 ships to sail to India through the Far East. The Fleet left Portugal on the 8th of July, 1497 and after many adventures, anchored off Malindi on Easter Sunday 15th April, 1498. Read More…
**The Portuguese Chapel**
The Portuguese presence in Malindi began with the arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498. On his second voyage to India, he left a group of solders in Malindi and a Chapel built in the style of that of the Navigator`s at Sagres in Portugal and a Portuguese` factory ‘or trading base which included store houses, barracks, residences and offices. Read More..
**The House of Columns (Malindi Museum)**
Though the date of construction of this unique structure is not known, it is known that it was used by Adulhussein Gulamhussein & Co. There is photographic evidence of its existence in 1891 when W. Fitzgerald took a picture of it from on board the IBEA’s coasting steamer, the Henry Wright, the boat that took him up to the coast from Mombasa to Lamu during his survey of the agricultural potential of the Kenya Coast. Read More..
**The Malindi Heritage Complex Museum**
This building was constructed in early 1890`s for the Imperial British East Africa Company ( IBEA Co.) which by British Royal Charter took over for 50 years the Sultan of Zanzibar`s mainland concession from Kipini to Vanga ( the coastal strip ). Mr. Bell Smith, an employee of IBEA Co., oversaw the construction of the building, known then as the District Collector`s Office, to serve as the company’s first office. Read More..

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
**Malindi Museum Heritage Complex**  
 [Wikimedia | © OpenStreetMap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#/map/0 "Show in full screen")  
Established May 10, 2004;22 years ago  
Coordinates3°12′57″S 40°07′19″E / 3.215922°S 40.121813°E  
Visitors 20,990 (2014)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-1)  
OwnerNational Museums of Kenya
**Malindi Museum** is a museum located in Malindi, Kenya. It has control over four main heritage sites: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and The Heritage Complex museum.

In 1991 the Malindi Museum Society was formed to support the policy of the National Museums of Kenya to acquire a historic building in Malindi that could be turned into a museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-2) Malindi's first museum building was opened in 2004, located in a two story building dating from 1891 known as The House of Columns. The building was constructed by Adulhussein Gulamhussein.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-3) The Bohra community sold the building for 2,000 English pounds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4) The building operated as an Indian trading center since its establishment in 1891.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) The building that houses the museum was used as Malindi's first native hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-6) On the east facade there is a colonnade featuring five round pillars. The building served as a hospital and headquarters of the Department of Fisheries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-7) In 1991, it was declared a national monument.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-8) In 1999 the House of Columns was transferred to the National Museum of Kenya and a restoration opened in 2004 as museum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9)

In 2013 Malindi Museum acquired a second set of buildings: the former offices of the District Commissioner, about 300 metres northwest along Silversand Road. This is now known as Malindi Museum Heritage Complex, the main building of which houses the ethnographic collections.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-10) Malindi Museum also has responsibility for two other heritage sites in the town: The Vasco da Gama Pillar and The Portuguese Chapel.
Coelacanth in The House of Columns
The Heritage Complex museum contains various historical artefacts from Malindi.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-11) The museum has exhibits containing traditional objects such as musical instruments, tools and costumes. On the ethnographic section, the museum contains various artefacts of the Mijikenda peoples who are ethnic groups inhabiting the Kenyan coast, including wooden totems,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) as well as ancient artifacts that belonged to Arabs who settled in Malindi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-12) In addition, the museum features artefacts from other communities that inhabit the Kenyan coast, as well as objects from the Swahili civilization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-13) The museum features exhibits about fish species and the history of Malindi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-14)

The House of Columns features temporary exhibits including famous _Malindi Coelacanth_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9) The museum also contains artifacts related to the explorer Vasco da Gama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-15)The House of Columns has exhibits from the Portuguese period of Kenya's coastal zone, as well as photographs of some of the country's archeological sites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-16) In addition, the museum owns the Webb Memorial Library which has books on the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-17)
A single ticket currently (2023) covers the four sites under the control of Malindi Museum. These are: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and the Malindi Museum Heritage Complex.

# Malindi Museum Day Tour
### Malindi Museum Day Tour - Old Town | Vasco da Gama Pillar & Portuguese Chapel
**Our Malindi Museum Day tour** combines a visit to the Malindi Museum, a stroll through **Malindi’s old town**, a visit to **Vasco da Gama’s pillar**, and the **Portuguese chapel**.
The Museum is located east of Malindi town, next to Uhuru Gardens, along the seafront, and a few meters from Malindi jetty and Fish Market.
The museum also serves as an information center, where visitors can find more information about attractions and events in Malindi. You also get to visit the famous Vasco da Gama Pillar, which was erected by the Portuguese explorer **Vasco da Gama** as a navigational aid in 1498.
The coral column, topped with a cross of Lisbon stone, is one of the most popular landmarks on the Kenyan Coast.
The other attraction you will visit, the Portuguese Chapel, was also built by Vasco da Gama and is the first Christian place of worship in East Africa.

# Malindi Museum Day Tour
### **Malindi Museum Day Tour Itinerary**
#### **Morning: Historical Circuit**
**0900 Hours – Malindi Museum (House of Columns)**: Start at this 19th-century double-story building. Key exhibits include the Malindi Coelacanth (a 400-million-year-old “living fossil”) and artifacts related to Vasco da Gama’s visit.
**1030 Hours – Portuguese Chapel**: Visit one of the oldest Christian churches in East Africa, built by Portuguese settlers in the 15th century. It features original walls, an altar, and a cemetery for early European settlers.
**1115 Hours – Vasco da Gama Pillar:** Head to the seafront to see the white coral pillar erected by the explorer in 1498. It offers panoramic views of the Indian Ocean and serves as a navigational landmark for ships traveling to India.
**Lunch & Culture
12:30 PM – Lunch:** Popular options include local seafood at The Crab Shack (Mida Creek) or Italian-influenced coastal dishes at I Love Pizza or Old Man and the Sea in Malindi town.
**1400 Hours – Malindi Old Town & Market:** Take a guided walk through narrow alleys to see Swahili-style houses with carved wooden doors. Visit the Malindi Maasai Market to shop for traditional wood carvings, jewelry, and handmade souvenirs

# Malindi Museum Day Tour
### **Malindi Museum Day Tour Itinerary**
#### **Afternoon Extensions (Optional) visit**
✓ Gede Ruins
✓Hell’s Kitchen
✓ Falconry Of Kenya Ltd
**Malindi Museum Day Tour**combines a visit to the Malindi Museum, a stroll through Malindi’s old town, a visit to Vasco da Gama’s pillar, and the Portuguese chapel built before St. Francis Xavier visited Malindi in 1542.
Malindi Museum is located east of Malindi town, next to Uhuru Gardens on Uhuru Road, along the seafront, and a few meters from Malindi jetty and Fish Market. The museum doubles as an information center where visitors are able to find more information on attractions and happenings in Malindi.
The MalindiMuseum building is dubbed as “House of Columns”and is believed to have been built by local traders and acted as a hospital until 1952 and then as the Malindi Fisheries Office.
Sir Richard Leakey then handed over the building to the National Museums of Kenya in 1999. With life-size models of humans, houses, musical instruments as well and household instruments, the Malindi Museum is indeed a reservoir of Swahili history.
There are also lots of written historical facts which are framed on the walls within the building. Many exhibits in the museum tell the story of Malindi especially the cast of a coelacanth fish which was caught off the coast of Malindi in 2001.
The earliest coelacanth fossils date back 400 million years ago. Enjoy our Malindi Museum Tour.

# Malindi Museum Day Tour
### Malindi Museum Day Tour - Old Town | Vasco da Gama Pillar & Portuguese Chapel
**Our Malindi Museum Day tour** combines a visit to the Malindi Museum, a stroll through **Malindi’s old town**, a visit to **Vasco da Gama’s pillar**, and the **Portuguese chapel**.
The Museum is located east of Malindi town, next to Uhuru Gardens, along the seafront, and a few meters from Malindi jetty and Fish Market.
The museum also serves as an information center, where visitors can find more information about attractions and events in Malindi. You also get to visit the famous Vasco da Gama Pillar, which was erected by the Portuguese explorer **Vasco da Gama** as a navigational aid in 1498.
The coral column, topped with a cross of Lisbon stone, is one of the most popular landmarks on the Kenyan Coast.
The other attraction you will visit, the Portuguese Chapel, was also built by Vasco da Gama and is the first Christian place of worship in East Africa.

# Malindi Museum Day Tour
### **Malindi Museum Day Tour Itinerary**
#### **Morning: Historical Circuit**
**0900 Hours – Malindi Museum (House of Columns)**: Start at this 19th-century double-story building. Key exhibits include the Malindi Coelacanth (a 400-million-year-old “living fossil”) and artifacts related to Vasco da Gama’s visit.
**1030 Hours – Portuguese Chapel**: Visit one of the oldest Christian churches in East Africa, built by Portuguese settlers in the 15th century. It features original walls, an altar, and a cemetery for early European settlers.
**1115 Hours – Vasco da Gama Pillar:** Head to the seafront to see the white coral pillar erected by the explorer in 1498. It offers panoramic views of the Indian Ocean and serves as a navigational landmark for ships traveling to India.
**Lunch & Culture
12:30 PM – Lunch:** Popular options include local seafood at The Crab Shack (Mida Creek) or Italian-influenced coastal dishes at I Love Pizza or Old Man and the Sea in Malindi town.
**1400 Hours – Malindi Old Town & Market:** Take a guided walk through narrow alleys to see Swahili-style houses with carved wooden doors. Visit the Malindi Maasai Market to shop for traditional wood carvings, jewelry, and handmade souvenirs

**Malindi Museum Day Tour**combines a visit to the Malindi Museum, a stroll through Malindi’s old town, a visit to Vasco da Gama’s pillar, and the Portuguese chapel built before St. Francis Xavier visited Malindi in 1542.
Malindi Museum is located east of Malindi town, next to Uhuru Gardens on Uhuru Road, along the seafront, and a few meters from Malindi jetty and Fish Market. The museum doubles as an information center where visitors are able to find more information on attractions and happenings in Malindi.
The MalindiMuseum building is dubbed as “House of Columns”and is believed to have been built by local traders and acted as a hospital until 1952 and then as the Malindi Fisheries Office.
Sir Richard Leakey then handed over the building to the National Museums of Kenya in 1999. With life-size models of humans, houses, musical instruments as well and household instruments, the Malindi Museum is indeed a reservoir of Swahili history.
There are also lots of written historical facts which are framed on the walls within the building. Many exhibits in the museum tell the story of Malindi especially the cast of a coelacanth fish which was caught off the coast of Malindi in 2001.
The earliest coelacanth fossils date back 400 million years ago. Enjoy our Malindi Museum Tour.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
**Malindi Museum Heritage Complex**  
 [Wikimedia | © OpenStreetMap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#/map/0 "Show in full screen")  
Established May 10, 2004;22 years ago  
Coordinates3°12′57″S 40°07′19″E / 3.215922°S 40.121813°E  
Visitors 20,990 (2014)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-1)  
OwnerNational Museums of Kenya
**Malindi Museum** is a museum located in Malindi, Kenya. It has control over four main heritage sites: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and The Heritage Complex museum.
texts.1: In 1991 the Malindi Museum Society was formed to support the policy of the National Museums of Kenya to acquire a historic building in Malindi that could be turned into a museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-2) Malindi's first museum building was opened in 2004, located in a two story building dating from 1891 known as The House of Columns. The building was constructed by Adulhussein Gulamhussein.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-3) The Bohra community sold the building for 2,000 English pounds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4) The building operated as an Indian trading center since its establishment in 1891.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) The building that houses the museum was used as Malindi's first native hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-6) On the east facade there is a colonnade featuring five round pillars. The building served as a hospital and headquarters of the Department of Fisheries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-7) In 1991, it was declared a national monument.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-8) In 1999 the House of Columns was transferred to the National Museum of Kenya and a restoration opened in 2004 as museum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9)
texts.2:
In 2013 Malindi Museum acquired a second set of buildings: the former offices of the District Commissioner, about 300 metres northwest along Silversand Road. This is now known as Malindi Museum Heritage Complex, the main building of which houses the ethnographic collections.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-10) Malindi Museum also has responsibility for two other heritage sites in the town: The Vasco da Gama Pillar and The Portuguese Chapel.
Coelacanth in The House of Columns
The Heritage Complex museum contains various historical artefacts from Malindi.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-11) The museum has exhibits containing traditional objects such as musical instruments, tools and costumes. On the ethnographic section, the museum contains various artefacts of the Mijikenda peoples who are ethnic groups inhabiting the Kenyan coast, including wooden totems,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) as well as ancient artifacts that belonged to Arabs who settled in Malindi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-12) In addition, the museum features artefacts from other communities that inhabit the Kenyan coast, as well as objects from the Swahili civilization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-13) The museum features exhibits about fish species and the history of Malindi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-14)
texts.3:
The House of Columns features temporary exhibits including famous _Malindi Coelacanth_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9) The museum also contains artifacts related to the explorer Vasco da Gama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-15)The House of Columns has exhibits from the Portuguese period of Kenya's coastal zone, as well as photographs of some of the country's archeological sites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-16) In addition, the museum owns the Webb Memorial Library which has books on the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-17)
A single ticket currently (2023) covers the four sites under the control of Malindi Museum. These are: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and the Malindi Museum Heritage Complex.

**The Vasco Da Gama Pillar**
The 15th Century was an era of worldwide exploration by Portugal. Early in the Century, Portugal had conceived an idea of commemorating visits of Portuguese vessels in different domains. In 1497, King Dom Manuel of Portugal appointed Vasco da Gama to command a fleet of 4 ships to sail to India through the Far East. The Fleet left Portugal on the 8th of July, 1497 and after many adventures, anchored off Malindi on Easter Sunday 15th April, 1498. Read More…
**The Portuguese Chapel**
The Portuguese presence in Malindi began with the arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498. On his second voyage to India, he left a group of solders in Malindi and a Chapel built in the style of that of the Navigator`s at Sagres in Portugal and a Portuguese` factory ‘or trading base which included store houses, barracks, residences and offices. Read More..
**The House of Columns (Malindi Museum)**
Though the date of construction of this unique structure is not known, it is known that it was used by Adulhussein Gulamhussein & Co. There is photographic evidence of its existence in 1891 when W. Fitzgerald took a picture of it from on board the IBEA’s coasting steamer, the Henry Wright, the boat that took him up to the coast from Mombasa to Lamu during his survey of the agricultural potential of the Kenya Coast. Read More..
**The Malindi Heritage Complex Museum**
This building was constructed in early 1890`s for the Imperial British East Africa Company ( IBEA Co.) which by British Royal Charter took over for 50 years the Sultan of Zanzibar`s mainland concession from Kipini to Vanga ( the coastal strip ). Mr. Bell Smith, an employee of IBEA Co., oversaw the construction of the building, known then as the District Collector`s Office, to serve as the company’s first office. Read More..

opened.information:
Source: https://www.africanhistoryextra.com/p/the-lost-city-of-malindi-in-global
Title: The Lost City of Malindi in Global and African History (c. 850-1890 CE)
Chunks: 6,7,8,9
When the Portuguese fleet under Vasco de Gama first arrived on the Swahili coast in 1498, the Malindi sultan welcomed them as useful allies against its rival Mombasa, which had been attacked by the same fleet. The Sultan offered provisions for their four-month-long stay and an Indian pilot named Malemo Canaqua (not _Ahmed Ibn Majid_) to guide Vasco de Gama to India.26
According to Hernan Lopes de Castaneda’s description of Vasco Da Gama’s visit;
_**“The town is well built. The houses are of stone and mortar, handsome on the outside and furnished inside with many rich decorations and paintings. The natives of the land are dark-skinned, with woolly hair, but well disposed.**_
_**The foreign residents are Arabian Moors. The nobles wear clothes above the arms, and turbans with silk and gold tassels. Their arms are short swords, lances, daggers, and bows and arrows. The greater number of the merchants who live in this town are from Guzerat in the kingdom of Cambaya. Gold, silver, ambergris, ivory, tar, and wax are found in this country.”**_27
_**Vasco da Gama pillar at Malindi.**_
The alliance between Malindi and the Portuguese was mutually beneficial, providing a base of operations in exchange for military aid and a redirection of all coastal trade to Malindi.
Subsequent expeditions will reinforce this close collaboration and the advantage that Malindi could derive from it. The Malindi king sent his own envoy to Portugal in the company of Vasco Da Gama, and the envoy successfully returned with the fleet of Pedro Alvares Cabral in 1500, bringing letters from the King of Portugal.28
The sultan took the opportunity of Cabral’s fleet to India to complain about an incursion from Mombasa. In 1503, the city suffered another attack from Mombasa, and the Portuguese retaliated by blockading Mombasa. In 1505, the ruler of Mombasa was once again at war with Malindi, ostensibly over Malindi’s alliance with the Portuguese. Malindi defeated Mombasa, and the latter was sacked by the Portuguese forces under Francisco de Almeida, who also attacked Kilwa.29

According to Joao de Barros, there is little doubt that the innumerable conflicts between Swahili city-states predate the Portuguese arrival, and were caused by disputes over territorial claims which the Portuguese captains did not always perceive. Thus Mombasa and Malindi disputed in the early 16th century Kilifi and “Chiona”, dominions of Malindi according to its sovereign.30
In 1506, the Malindi sultan requested that the Portuguese fleet under Tristao da Cunha invade the neighboring city of Oja, described as a beautiful walled city (likely near the ruined site of Shaka). Contrary to the sultan’s claim that Oja resented Malindi for its alliance with the Portuguese, João de Barros suggests that the conflict predates the Portuguese incursion.31
In an exemplary letter concerning the attack on Mombasa in 1542, João de Sepúlveda reported that, _**“the King of Malindi asked me to destroy some neighboring place with whom he had been at war for many years, which I did.”**_ In the late 16th century, Malindians not only used the Portuguese to subdue and extract tribute from the island of Pemba, but also settled the island with members of the ruling Malindian Sultan’s family.32
_**Ruins of Shaka, Kenya.**_
_**Pillar tombs and mosque (in background),**_ Ras Mkumbuu, Pemba Island, Tanzania.
Malindi would remain the main base of operation for the Portuguese from 1509 to the founding of Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593.
A position of “captain of the coast of Malindi” (capittio da costa de Melinde) was put in place, and his office was mostly centered on issuing safe conducts to ships. The only military operations were all based on requests from Malindi and Zanzibar seeking to reduce Mombasa’s hegemony, but were often inconclusive given the lack of permanent garrisons before 1593.33
In 1585-9, the war between the Ottoman corsair Ali Bey with his allies at Mombasa and the Portuguese with Malindi ends with the defeat of the former, with assistance from the Segeju, a mainland African group.

The Segeju occupied Mombasa and Kilifi, apparently at the request of Malindi’s ally known as Watamu, and later handed Mombasa over to Malindi. The Malindi royal family then moved to the Portuguese fort at Mombasa, where it received a third of the revenue.34
_**Fort Jesus, Mombasa, Kenya**_. Image by World History Encyclopedia
The extent of Malindi’s international trade is revealed in Portuguese documents from India during this period.
In 1511, Malindi was included among several Swahili cities whose merchants were reported in the city of Malacca (in Malaysia) by Tome Pires, alongside Kilwa and Mogadishu.35
In 1515, the king of Malindi, Sheikh “Wagerage,” asked for authorization to send one of his ships to Goa. In 1586, Sultan Muhammad of Malindi sent a ship to the Portuguese settlement of Bassein. In 1596, the same king wrote to Philip II of Spain requesting free passage to the Portuguese outposts in India and a trading mission to China.36
In 1606, the Franciscan friars met a _mwalimu_, described as an “old Muslim Negro” and a “_Melindano_” (a native of the coast of Malindi) who in 1597 had guided the ship of Francisco da Gama, the future viceroy of India, from Mombasa to Goa.37 A letter written in 1619 mentions muslims from Malindi passing through the capital of the Estado in Goa, India.38
In 1694, the leader of the Swahili community in Goa was Faki Wali wa Mwinyi Matano, who was titled “Governor of the Moors of Malindi.”39 These may have been the same group as the government pensioners found in records at Goa dated to the early 17th century, who were from East Africa and were called ‘noblemen of Malindi’.40
_**Lamu Dhow in Malindi.**_
In Malindi, the continued influx of foreign merchants seems not to have altered its disadvantaged commercial position relative to Mombasa.

A small community of Portuguese merchants, settlers and priests was established in the city during the early 16th century. These seem to have become acculturated into the Swahili mode of commercial transactions based on personal ties and exchanges conducted in private residences rather than large markets.41
Indian Merchants from the city of Cambay in Gujarat were found at Malindi and many other towns on the East African coast at the time of the Portuguese arrival.42
Cabral’s account from 1500 found three large ships from Cambay at Malindi, each with a capacity of 1/3 of a ton. A report from 1517-18 mentions that the merchants of Malindi _**“are great barterers, and deal in cloth, gold, ivory, and divers other wares with the Moors and Heathen of the great kingdom of Cambaya; and to their haven come every year many ships with cargoes of merchandise, from which they get great store of gold, ivory, and wax.”**_43
Besides the Portuguese and Indians, a report from 1608 mentions the arrival of Hadrimi sharifs from Yemen who were _**“pale and white, differing very much from the color of the Moors [ie; Swahili]”**_; and could be found _**“among the principal gentlemen of the whole coast of Malindi”**_44
Historical traditions mention intermarriages with the ruling family of Pate and how the latter then supplanted the Bauri, the Shiraziclan who formerly had ruled at Ozi and Malindi.45 The ascendant clan with links to Pate, who were known as the waVumba, after their main town that is today located at the Kenya/Tanzania border, subsumed several of the older towns in the region and reinvigorated external trade.46
The Sharifs, alongside the Swahili of Malindi, were involved in trade from northern Madagascar.47
_**Northern Madagascar and the Swahili Coast.**_ Map by G Campbell

Title: Malindi: Ancient Coastal Town of Kenya
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
8 min read
Nov 19, 2024
--
--
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Young people playing football at Malindi Beach. Photo: Samuel Phillips
T ourism in Kenya is very vibrant and even though the country has its ups and downs and areas that need working on, it still remains one of the most visited touring countries in Africa. Tourism accounts for about 10 to 24% of Kenya’s GDP.
When you hear of tourism in Kenya, one of the many places that quickly comes to mind is the legendary Maasai Mara, especially because of the magnificence of the Maasai people whose ancient nomadic culture and way of life are so popular globally that you can’t miss hearing about them even if you have never been to Kenya. In my case, I read about the Massai in my history class in my secondary school days. Interestingly, back then the name Kenya never stayed in my mind but the name Maasai stuck like glue.
And then you have Mt Kenya, the Aberdares, Nairobi National Park, Tsavo National Park, Amboseli, Marsabit National Park in the north of Kenya close to Kenya’s border with Ethiopia, the list is very long. We lived in Marsabit for about five months. Most of these tourist places are within the inland of Kenya and they all have their unique beauty and how they influence the thoughts of tourists who come into Kenya at various times of the year. I have only visited a few places myself.
The coast of Kenya is also blessed with several tourist towns and attractions. One of the coastal legends is easily Mombasa Old Town where you find Fort Jesus and there are several other interesting sites located in the coastal counties of the country.
These include Malindi town in Kilifi County, which is just after Mombasa County.
**History of Malindi**
Malindi, located about 120 km northeast of Mombasa, is one of the most famous tourist towns along the coast and is now the second largest city on the Indian Ocean coast of Kenya after Mombasa. The population was 208,000 inhabitants in 2009 and is located in County Kilifi which, again in 2009, had a population of 1.11 million.

It is an ancient coastal town founded around the 1st century AD as an Arabic settlement and trading post, probably at Mambrui, North of the river Sabaki.
Although known under the Portuguese name of Melinde, some claim the origin of the Swahili name of Mali Ndi which means “lot of wealth”.
The Arabs established the current Malindi in the early 13th century. In 1414 the King of Malindi initiated diplomatic relations with China during the voyages of the Explorer Zheng He.
The April 15, 1498 (the year 918 of the Arab calendar) the Sheikh of Malindi, al-Bauri, at war with Mombasa, welcomed the great Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama, who anchored three ships in the port of Malindi: São Gabriel, a caracca commanded by Vasco himself, São Rafael under the command of his brother Paulo and Berrio (later renamed São Miguel) commanded by Nicolau Coelho. It is said that Vasco da Gama never left São Gabriel, a ship of about 200 tons with square sails and large red crosses.
The following year the East African ports were opened officially to Europe so the Portuguese established a trading post. At that time, the city was a wealthy Kingdom. The residents mingled with Arabs who were the ruling class and the city was surrounded by walls. The Arabs lived inside the walls in stone houses, while Africans lived mainly in mud huts and trellises of canes with palm-thatched roofs.
The economy consisted of agriculture and trade with various ports in the Indian Ocean. Near Malindi, there were large fruit plantations (lemons, oranges), coconut palms, sugar cane, vegetables, and livestock. Slaves and ivory were exported. The city was an important port in East Africa.
In the early 16th century, the Portuguese chose Malindi as a supply station for the Portuguese ships, so they built their own administration, gas stations, and houses for their officials. In 1518 Mozambique took over the role of Malindi as a replenishment station for Portuguese ships because the Portuguese had trouble defending Malindi.
With the construction of the Portuguese Fort Jesus in the nearby town of Mombasa (1593) Malindi began its decline. The Portuguese administration and customs were transferred to Mombasa and after 1666 the Portuguese lost complete control of the city.

The Sultan of Zanzibar Majir refounded Malindi in 1861 and its wealth increased between 1861 and 1890. Arab Governors appointed by the Sultan of Zanzibar and supported by a garrison of between thirty and one hundred and fifty Baluchi soldiers administered the city. After 1873 the slave trade became illegal, leading to a decline in the agricultural economy, so the Arabs were willing to take part in the local wage-based Africans. The Sultan of Zanzibar subsequently rented its territories, which included the Malindi region, to the British East Africa Association (see Republican Council of Mombasa). (**Source****)**
**Italian Influence**
In early August of 2024, my family and I moved from Kaya Kinondo Sacred Forest in Kwale County to Malindi.
At first impression, the town looked just like every normal coastal town you will find in Africa; windy, hot, humid, dry, and quite noisy because it’s a tourist destination and then you find reminiscence of ancient times in the relics scattered across the area. I cannot tell when this became a thing in this coastal Kenyan town, but one of the very first things you also notice is the heavy presence of Europeans, especially Italians. I know this is a tourist destination, and the presence of Europeans should not be surprising, but beyond that, it’s in the public domain that Malindi is a town largely influenced by the Italian culture, and in some quarters, some think the international airport in Malindi, even though it’s small in size compared to many international airports in Kenya, was established because of the Italian mafia. How many of these are real stories, I cannot tell you. But you can see the town crawling with stores and businesses with Italian names and Italians patronizing their own.

## Get Samuel Phillips’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.
Remember me for faster sign in
Just like in Diani, in Kwale county, you find scores of old European men dating young African ladies or even girls, and the same with old European women dating or hanging out with young African men. And some, I guess, are actually married. And there are lots of mixed-race children, I believe, from such relationships.
**Places to visit in Malindi**
Malindi definitely has its own unique vibe and should be explored for all the fun places. Here are a few places you can consider visiting when you come here.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Goodbyte Restaurant, opposite Malindi Airport, Malindi. Photo by Samuel Phillips
**1. Goodbyte Restaurant:**
For me, I think the best place to visit in any new environment is where you get the best food for a reasonably good price.
On the day we arrived in Malindi, while still making our way to the apartment that we were to rent, we decided to stop for some food in town. We found a restaurant called Goodbyte Restaurant just opposite the Malindi Airport. This restaurant not only serves good food, but their attendants are also very skillful in handling your order. Since moving to Malindi (close to three months now), we have visited this restaurant about three times and there are no disappointments. At each visit, we were served by a gentleman named John. He has a gentle demeanor for real. Even when my young son broke a glass, John showed no unnecessary reaction, he remained cool with his gentle smile. He quickly moved us to another table to create room for the floor to be cleaned, brought our son another glass, with a smile. I am not even sure if we were charged for the broken glass.
Our order that day was Biryani rice with fried chicken dipped in tomato stew. The spice was very coastal and it hit the right places.
The restaurant is located at The Festival Mall, opposite Malindi Airport.

Arab Governors appointed by the Sultan of Zanzibar and supported by a garrison of between thirty and one hundred and fifty Baluchi soldiers administered the city. After 1873 the slave trade became illegal, leading to a decline in the agricultural economy, so the Arabs were willing to take part in the local wage-based Africans. The Sultan of Zanzibar subsequently rented its territories, which included the Malindi region, to the British East Africa Association (see Republican Council of Mombasa). (**Source****)**
**Italian Influence**
In early August of 2024, my family and I moved from Kaya Kinondo Sacred Forest in Kwale County to Malindi.
At first impression, the town looked just like every normal coastal town you will find in Africa; windy, hot, humid, dry, and quite noisy because it’s a tourist destination and then you find reminiscence of ancient times in the relics scattered across the area. I cannot tell when this became a thing in this coastal Kenyan town, but one of the very first things you also notice is the heavy presence of Europeans, especially Italians. I know this is a tourist destination, and the presence of Europeans should not be surprising, but beyond that, it’s in the public domain that Malindi is a town largely influenced by the Italian culture, and in some quarters, some think the international airport in Malindi, even though it’s small in size compared to many international airports in Kenya, was established because of the Italian mafia. How many of these are real stories, I cannot tell you. But you can see the town crawling with stores and businesses with Italian names and Italians patronizing their own.

Just like in Diani, in Kwale county, you find scores of old European men dating young African ladies or even girls, and the same with old European women dating or hanging out with young African men. And some, I guess, are actually married. And there are lots of mixed-race children, I believe, from such relationships.
**Places to visit in Malindi**
Malindi definitely has its own unique vibe and should be explored for all the fun places. Here are a few places you can consider visiting when you come here.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Goodbyte Restaurant, opposite Malindi Airport, Malindi. Photo by Samuel Phillips
**1. Goodbyte Restaurant:**
For me, I think the best place to visit in any new environment is where you get the best food for a reasonably good price.
On the day we arrived in Malindi, while still making our way to the apartment that we were to rent, we decided to stop for some food in town. We found a restaurant called Goodbyte Restaurant just opposite the Malindi Airport. This restaurant not only serves good food, but their attendants are also very skillful in handling your order. Since moving to Malindi (close to three months now), we have visited this restaurant about three times and there are no disappointments. At each visit, we were served by a gentleman named John. He has a gentle demeanor for real. Even when my young son broke a glass, John showed no unnecessary reaction, he remained cool with his gentle smile. He quickly moved us to another table to create room for the floor to be cleaned, brought our son another glass, with a smile. I am not even sure if we were charged for the broken glass.
Our order that day was Biryani rice with fried chicken dipped in tomato stew. The spice was very coastal and it hit the right places.
The restaurant is located at The Festival Mall, opposite Malindi Airport.

texts.6:
When the Portuguese fleet under Vasco de Gama first arrived on the Swahili coast in 1498, the Malindi sultan welcomed them as useful allies against its rival Mombasa, which had been attacked by the same fleet. The Sultan offered provisions for their four-month-long stay and an Indian pilot named Malemo Canaqua (not _Ahmed Ibn Majid_) to guide Vasco de Gama to India.26
According to Hernan Lopes de Castaneda’s description of Vasco Da Gama’s visit;
_**“The town is well built. The houses are of stone and mortar, handsome on the outside and furnished inside with many rich decorations and paintings. The natives of the land are dark-skinned, with woolly hair, but well disposed.**_
_**The foreign residents are Arabian Moors. The nobles wear clothes above the arms, and turbans with silk and gold tassels. Their arms are short swords, lances, daggers, and bows and arrows. The greater number of the merchants who live in this town are from Guzerat in the kingdom of Cambaya. Gold, silver, ambergris, ivory, tar, and wax are found in this country.”**_27
_**Vasco da Gama pillar at Malindi.**_
The alliance between Malindi and the Portuguese was mutually beneficial, providing a base of operations in exchange for military aid and a redirection of all coastal trade to Malindi.
Subsequent expeditions will reinforce this close collaboration and the advantage that Malindi could derive from it. The Malindi king sent his own envoy to Portugal in the company of Vasco Da Gama, and the envoy successfully returned with the fleet of Pedro Alvares Cabral in 1500, bringing letters from the King of Portugal.28
The sultan took the opportunity of Cabral’s fleet to India to complain about an incursion from Mombasa. In 1503, the city suffered another attack from Mombasa, and the Portuguese retaliated by blockading Mombasa. In 1505, the ruler of Mombasa was once again at war with Malindi, ostensibly over Malindi’s alliance with the Portuguese. Malindi defeated Mombasa, and the latter was sacked by the Portuguese forces under Francisco de Almeida, who also attacked Kilwa.29
texts.7:
According to Joao de Barros, there is little doubt that the innumerable conflicts between Swahili city-states predate the Portuguese arrival, and were caused by disputes over territorial claims which the Portuguese captains did not always perceive. Thus Mombasa and Malindi disputed in the early 16th century Kilifi and “Chiona”, dominions of Malindi according to its sovereign.30
In 1506, the Malindi sultan requested that the Portuguese fleet under Tristao da Cunha invade the neighboring city of Oja, described as a beautiful walled city (likely near the ruined site of Shaka). Contrary to the sultan’s claim that Oja resented Malindi for its alliance with the Portuguese, João de Barros suggests that the conflict predates the Portuguese incursion.31
In an exemplary letter concerning the attack on Mombasa in 1542, João de Sepúlveda reported that, _**“the King of Malindi asked me to destroy some neighboring place with whom he had been at war for many years, which I did.”**_ In the late 16th century, Malindians not only used the Portuguese to subdue and extract tribute from the island of Pemba, but also settled the island with members of the ruling Malindian Sultan’s family.32
_**Ruins of Shaka, Kenya.**_
_**Pillar tombs and mosque (in background),**_ Ras Mkumbuu, Pemba Island, Tanzania.
Malindi would remain the main base of operation for the Portuguese from 1509 to the founding of Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593.
A position of “captain of the coast of Malindi” (capittio da costa de Melinde) was put in place, and his office was mostly centered on issuing safe conducts to ships. The only military operations were all based on requests from Malindi and Zanzibar seeking to reduce Mombasa’s hegemony, but were often inconclusive given the lack of permanent garrisons before 1593.33
In 1585-9, the war between the Ottoman corsair Ali Bey with his allies at Mombasa and the Portuguese with Malindi ends with the defeat of the former, with assistance from the Segeju, a mainland African group.
texts.8:
The Segeju occupied Mombasa and Kilifi, apparently at the request of Malindi’s ally known as Watamu, and later handed Mombasa over to Malindi. The Malindi royal family then moved to the Portuguese fort at Mombasa, where it received a third of the revenue.34
_**Fort Jesus, Mombasa, Kenya**_. Image by World History Encyclopedia
The extent of Malindi’s international trade is revealed in Portuguese documents from India during this period.
In 1511, Malindi was included among several Swahili cities whose merchants were reported in the city of Malacca (in Malaysia) by Tome Pires, alongside Kilwa and Mogadishu.35
In 1515, the king of Malindi, Sheikh “Wagerage,” asked for authorization to send one of his ships to Goa. In 1586, Sultan Muhammad of Malindi sent a ship to the Portuguese settlement of Bassein. In 1596, the same king wrote to Philip II of Spain requesting free passage to the Portuguese outposts in India and a trading mission to China.36
In 1606, the Franciscan friars met a _mwalimu_, described as an “old Muslim Negro” and a “_Melindano_” (a native of the coast of Malindi) who in 1597 had guided the ship of Francisco da Gama, the future viceroy of India, from Mombasa to Goa.37 A letter written in 1619 mentions muslims from Malindi passing through the capital of the Estado in Goa, India.38
In 1694, the leader of the Swahili community in Goa was Faki Wali wa Mwinyi Matano, who was titled “Governor of the Moors of Malindi.”39 These may have been the same group as the government pensioners found in records at Goa dated to the early 17th century, who were from East Africa and were called ‘noblemen of Malindi’.40
_**Lamu Dhow in Malindi.**_
In Malindi, the continued influx of foreign merchants seems not to have altered its disadvantaged commercial position relative to Mombasa.
texts.9:
A small community of Portuguese merchants, settlers and priests was established in the city during the early 16th century. These seem to have become acculturated into the Swahili mode of commercial transactions based on personal ties and exchanges conducted in private residences rather than large markets.41
Indian Merchants from the city of Cambay in Gujarat were found at Malindi and many other towns on the East African coast at the time of the Portuguese arrival.42
Cabral’s account from 1500 found three large ships from Cambay at Malindi, each with a capacity of 1/3 of a ton. A report from 1517-18 mentions that the merchants of Malindi _**“are great barterers, and deal in cloth, gold, ivory, and divers other wares with the Moors and Heathen of the great kingdom of Cambaya; and to their haven come every year many ships with cargoes of merchandise, from which they get great store of gold, ivory, and wax.”**_43
Besides the Portuguese and Indians, a report from 1608 mentions the arrival of Hadrimi sharifs from Yemen who were _**“pale and white, differing very much from the color of the Moors [ie; Swahili]”**_; and could be found _**“among the principal gentlemen of the whole coast of Malindi”**_44
Historical traditions mention intermarriages with the ruling family of Pate and how the latter then supplanted the Bauri, the Shiraziclan who formerly had ruled at Ozi and Malindi.45 The ascendant clan with links to Pate, who were known as the waVumba, after their main town that is today located at the Kenya/Tanzania border, subsumed several of the older towns in the region and reinvigorated external trade.46
The Sharifs, alongside the Swahili of Malindi, were involved in trade from northern Madagascar.47
_**Northern Madagascar and the Swahili Coast.**_ Map by G Campbell
