Malindi Museum preserves the rich history of Malindi through four important heritage sites including the Vasco da Gama Pillar, Portuguese Chapel, House of Columns, and the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum.
Malindi Museum is one of Kenya’s most important coastal heritage institutions, preserving centuries of history, cultural exchange, maritime exploration, and architectural development along the East African coast. Located in the historic town of Malindi, the museum manages four significant heritage attractions that collectively tell the story of one of the oldest and most influential settlements on the Swahili Coast.
Unlike many museums that operate from a single site, Malindi Museum is a network of interconnected heritage attractions. These include the famous Vasco da Gama Pillar, the historic Portuguese Chapel, the House of Columns, and the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum. Together, these sites provide visitors with a comprehensive understanding of Malindi’s role in regional and global history.
For centuries, Malindi served as a thriving center of trade, diplomacy, cultural exchange, and maritime activity. Merchants, explorers, sailors, religious leaders, and travelers from Africa, Arabia, Persia, India, and Europe all contributed to shaping the identity of the town. Today, Malindi Museum preserves this remarkable legacy through carefully curated collections, historic monuments, and educational programs.
Whether you are interested in Swahili culture, Portuguese exploration, maritime history, colonial architecture, archaeology, or coastal heritage, Malindi Museum offers an engaging journey through some of the most fascinating chapters of East African history.

## About Malindi Museum
Malindi Museum is operated by the National Museums of Kenya and serves as the primary institution responsible for preserving and interpreting the heritage of Malindi and its surrounding region. The museum oversees four major heritage sites that collectively represent different periods and aspects of the town’s history.
These sites allow visitors to explore the evolution of Malindi from a medieval Swahili trading settlement to an important stop along international maritime routes and later a colonial administrative center. The museum's collections and monuments highlight the interactions between local communities and foreign visitors who arrived on the East African coast over several centuries.
Through exhibitions, research, conservation work, and public education programs, Malindi Museum helps preserve the cultural identity of the Kenyan coast while making this heritage accessible to local communities and international visitors alike.

## History of Malindi Museum
The modern history of Malindi Museum began in 1991 when the Malindi Museum Society was established to support efforts by the National Museums of Kenya to preserve an important historic building within the town. The goal was to create a museum that would protect and showcase the region’s unique historical and cultural heritage.
The first museum facility was established within the House of Columns, a distinctive two-storey building dating back to 1891. This historic structure became the foundation of the museum and remains one of its most recognizable landmarks today.
Originally constructed by Adulhussein Gulamhussein, the House of Columns served various functions throughout its history. It operated as an Indian trading center, later became Malindi’s first native hospital, and subsequently housed government departments before eventually being preserved as a heritage monument.
In recognition of its historical significance, the building was declared a national monument in 1991. It was later transferred to the National Museums of Kenya, restored, and officially opened as a museum in 2004.
A major expansion occurred in 2013 when Malindi Museum acquired a second heritage property consisting of the former District Commissioner’s offices. This site became known as the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum and significantly expanded the museum’s exhibition and educational capabilities.
Today, Malindi Museum continues to grow as a leading center for heritage preservation, research, and cultural education on the Kenyan coast.

## The Vasco da Gama Pillar
The Vasco da Gama Pillar is one of the most famous historical monuments on the East African coast and one of the most recognizable landmarks in Malindi. Standing on a rocky outcrop overlooking the Indian Ocean, the pillar serves as a powerful reminder of the Age of Exploration and the maritime connections that linked Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East during the late fifteenth century.
For more than five centuries, the monument has stood as a symbol of Malindi's importance within international trade networks and its role in one of the most significant voyages in world history. Today, it remains one of the most visited heritage attractions managed by Malindi Museum and continues to attract historians, researchers, students, and tourists from around the world.
The pillar is widely regarded as one of the oldest surviving European monuments in sub-Saharan Africa and occupies an important place in both Kenyan and global history.

## Vasco da Gama's Arrival in Malindi
The story of the Vasco da Gama Pillar begins during the great era of Portuguese exploration. During the fifteenth century, Portugal became one of the leading maritime powers in Europe and invested heavily in voyages aimed at discovering new trade routes and expanding commercial opportunities.
In 1497, King Dom Manuel I of Portugal appointed the explorer Vasco da Gama to command an expedition tasked with finding a sea route from Europe to India. This ambitious mission would ultimately transform global trade and establish new connections between continents.
On 8 July 1497, Vasco da Gama departed Portugal with a fleet of four ships. After months of navigating unfamiliar waters and overcoming numerous challenges, the expedition reached the East African coast.
On Easter Sunday, 15 April 1498, Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored off the coast of Malindi. The arrival marked a historic moment not only for Portugal but also for the wider world, as it represented a crucial step toward establishing direct maritime trade between Europe and Asia.
Malindi played a particularly important role in the success of the expedition. The town's leaders welcomed the Portuguese visitors and provided assistance that proved essential for the continuation of the voyage toward India.

## Why Malindi Was Important to Portuguese Explorers
During the late fifteenth century, Malindi was one of the most prosperous and influential Swahili city-states along the East African coast. Its strategic location made it an important center for trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange.
Merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, and other regions regularly visited Malindi, contributing to a vibrant cosmopolitan society connected to the wider Indian Ocean trading world.
For Portuguese explorers seeking routes to Asia, Malindi offered a safe harbor, valuable local knowledge, and opportunities to establish diplomatic relationships. The town's rulers recognized the potential benefits of engaging with the newcomers and supported their journey.
Historical accounts indicate that Vasco da Gama received assistance from experienced navigators familiar with the monsoon wind systems of the Indian Ocean. This knowledge helped guide the Portuguese fleet across the ocean toward the western coast of India.
Without the support received in Malindi, the success of the expedition might have been far less certain.

## The Purpose of the Vasco da Gama Pillar
During this period, Portuguese explorers commonly erected stone markers known as padrões to commemorate important voyages and assert the presence of Portugal in newly visited territories.
These monuments served several purposes. They acted as navigational markers, symbols of diplomatic relationships, records of exploration, and visible reminders of Portuguese maritime achievements.
The Vasco da Gama Pillar in Malindi was erected as part of this tradition and became one of the most enduring symbols of Portugal's age of exploration.
Its survival over more than five centuries makes it one of the most remarkable historical monuments associated with early European exploration beyond Europe itself.

## Architecture and Design of the Vasco da Gama Pillar
The monument is constructed from coral stone, a material widely used along the East African coast because of its availability and durability. Positioned on a promontory overlooking the sea, the pillar was carefully placed to be visible to vessels approaching the coast.
Its elevated location provides spectacular views of the Indian Ocean and helps visitors appreciate the maritime setting that shaped the history of Malindi.
Although relatively simple in appearance compared with later colonial monuments, the pillar carries immense historical significance because of its direct association with one of the most important periods of global exploration.
The site also offers excellent opportunities for photography and remains one of the most iconic attractions within Malindi.

## The Vasco da Gama Pillar and Global History
The arrival of Vasco da Gama in East Africa formed part of a broader process that reshaped global trade, politics, and cultural exchange. The successful establishment of a sea route linking Europe and Asia fundamentally altered patterns of commerce and international relations.
Through this connection, goods, technologies, ideas, and people moved across vast distances with increasing frequency. The Indian Ocean became an even more important arena for interaction among civilizations from Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
The Vasco da Gama Pillar serves as a tangible reminder of these transformations and provides visitors with an opportunity to reflect on how global history has been shaped by exploration, trade, and cultural exchange.
As one of the oldest surviving monuments associated with this era, the pillar occupies a unique place within the heritage of Kenya and the wider world.

## Maritime Heritage at Malindi Museum
The Indian Ocean has always played a central role in the history of Malindi. Maritime heritage exhibitions explore the relationship between coastal communities and the sea, highlighting activities such as navigation, fishing, shipbuilding, and long-distance trade.
The exhibits demonstrate how generations of sailors and merchants used monsoon winds to connect East Africa with destinations across the Indian Ocean. These maritime networks facilitated cultural exchange and economic development while shaping the identity of coastal settlements.
Visitors learn about traditional seafaring technologies, trade routes, and the importance of maritime resources to local communities. These insights help explain why coastal towns such as Malindi became significant centers of commerce and cultural interaction.
The maritime collections also complement the stories associated with the Vasco da Gama Pillar and Portuguese exploration, creating a broader understanding of the region's relationship with the sea.

## The Webb Memorial Library
One of the lesser-known but highly valuable resources associated with Malindi Museum is the Webb Memorial Library. This specialized library contains publications, reference materials, historical records, and research resources relating to the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.
The library supports researchers, students, historians, and heritage professionals seeking deeper knowledge about the region. Its collections provide access to information that may not be readily available elsewhere.
Subjects covered include archaeology, architecture, maritime history, ethnography, environmental studies, cultural heritage management, and regional history. These resources contribute to ongoing research and support educational activities associated with the museum.
For scholars interested in the Swahili Coast, the library represents an important center of knowledge and documentation.

## Educational Programs and Public Learning
Education is one of the core functions of Malindi Museum. Through exhibitions, guided tours, workshops, school visits, and public programs, the museum helps make history and cultural heritage accessible to diverse audiences.
Students benefit from opportunities to engage directly with historical objects and heritage sites, while teachers can use museum resources to enrich classroom learning. Visitors of all ages gain valuable insights into the cultural and historical development of the Kenyan coast.
The museum's educational mission extends beyond formal learning by encouraging public appreciation of heritage and promoting awareness of conservation issues.
By fostering curiosity and understanding, Malindi Museum contributes to preserving cultural knowledge while inspiring future generations to value and protect their heritage.

## Why Malindi Museum's Collections Matter
The collections preserved by Malindi Museum are important not only because they document the past but also because they help communities understand their identity and cultural heritage. They provide tangible evidence of historical experiences, achievements, and connections that continue to shape contemporary society.
Through careful conservation and interpretation, the museum ensures that these valuable resources remain available for future generations. Visitors leave with a deeper appreciation of the diverse cultures, traditions, and historical events that have contributed to the unique character of Malindi and the Kenyan coast.
As a result, Malindi Museum plays a crucial role in preserving memory, supporting education, promoting research, and strengthening cultural understanding both within Kenya and internationally.

## Visitor Experience at Malindi Museum
A visit to Malindi Museum offers much more than a traditional museum experience. Because the institution manages four separate heritage attractions, visitors have the opportunity to explore multiple aspects of coastal history through a single admission ticket.
Guests can begin their journey at the House of Columns and the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum before continuing to the Vasco da Gama Pillar and Portuguese Chapel. Together, these sites provide a comprehensive overview of Malindi's development from a Swahili trading settlement to an internationally connected port town that played a role in some of the most significant events of global maritime history.

Malindi Museum preserves the rich history of Malindi through four important heritage sites including the Vasco da Gama Pillar, Portuguese Chapel, House of Columns, and the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum.
Malindi Museum is one of Kenya’s most important coastal heritage institutions, preserving centuries of history, cultural exchange, maritime exploration, and architectural development along the East African coast. Located in the historic town of Malindi, the museum manages four significant heritage attractions that collectively tell the story of one of the oldest and most influential settlements on the Swahili Coast.
Unlike many museums that operate from a single site, Malindi Museum is a network of interconnected heritage attractions. These include the famous Vasco da Gama Pillar, the historic Portuguese Chapel, the House of Columns, and the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum. Together, these sites provide visitors with a comprehensive understanding of Malindi’s role in regional and global history.
For centuries, Malindi served as a thriving center of trade, diplomacy, cultural exchange, and maritime activity. Merchants, explorers, sailors, religious leaders, and travelers from Africa, Arabia, Persia, India, and Europe all contributed to shaping the identity of the town. Today, Malindi Museum preserves this remarkable legacy through carefully curated collections, historic monuments, and educational programs.
Whether you are interested in Swahili culture, Portuguese exploration, maritime history, colonial architecture, archaeology, or coastal heritage, Malindi Museum offers an engaging journey through some of the most fascinating chapters of East African history.
texts.1:
## About Malindi Museum
Malindi Museum is operated by the National Museums of Kenya and serves as the primary institution responsible for preserving and interpreting the heritage of Malindi and its surrounding region. The museum oversees four major heritage sites that collectively represent different periods and aspects of the town’s history.
These sites allow visitors to explore the evolution of Malindi from a medieval Swahili trading settlement to an important stop along international maritime routes and later a colonial administrative center. The museum's collections and monuments highlight the interactions between local communities and foreign visitors who arrived on the East African coast over several centuries.
Through exhibitions, research, conservation work, and public education programs, Malindi Museum helps preserve the cultural identity of the Kenyan coast while making this heritage accessible to local communities and international visitors alike.
texts.2:
## History of Malindi Museum
The modern history of Malindi Museum began in 1991 when the Malindi Museum Society was established to support efforts by the National Museums of Kenya to preserve an important historic building within the town. The goal was to create a museum that would protect and showcase the region’s unique historical and cultural heritage.
The first museum facility was established within the House of Columns, a distinctive two-storey building dating back to 1891. This historic structure became the foundation of the museum and remains one of its most recognizable landmarks today.
Originally constructed by Adulhussein Gulamhussein, the House of Columns served various functions throughout its history. It operated as an Indian trading center, later became Malindi’s first native hospital, and subsequently housed government departments before eventually being preserved as a heritage monument.
In recognition of its historical significance, the building was declared a national monument in 1991. It was later transferred to the National Museums of Kenya, restored, and officially opened as a museum in 2004.
A major expansion occurred in 2013 when Malindi Museum acquired a second heritage property consisting of the former District Commissioner’s offices. This site became known as the Malindi Heritage Complex Museum and significantly expanded the museum’s exhibition and educational capabilities.
Today, Malindi Museum continues to grow as a leading center for heritage preservation, research, and cultural education on the Kenyan coast.
texts.3:
## The Vasco da Gama Pillar
The Vasco da Gama Pillar is one of the most famous historical monuments on the East African coast and one of the most recognizable landmarks in Malindi. Standing on a rocky outcrop overlooking the Indian Ocean, the pillar serves as a powerful reminder of the Age of Exploration and the maritime connections that linked Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East during the late fifteenth century.
For more than five centuries, the monument has stood as a symbol of Malindi's importance within international trade networks and its role in one of the most significant voyages in world history. Today, it remains one of the most visited heritage attractions managed by Malindi Museum and continues to attract historians, researchers, students, and tourists from around the world.
The pillar is widely regarded as one of the oldest surviving European monuments in sub-Saharan Africa and occupies an important place in both Kenyan and global history.
texts.4:
## Vasco da Gama's Arrival in Malindi
The story of the Vasco da Gama Pillar begins during the great era of Portuguese exploration. During the fifteenth century, Portugal became one of the leading maritime powers in Europe and invested heavily in voyages aimed at discovering new trade routes and expanding commercial opportunities.
In 1497, King Dom Manuel I of Portugal appointed the explorer Vasco da Gama to command an expedition tasked with finding a sea route from Europe to India. This ambitious mission would ultimately transform global trade and establish new connections between continents.
On 8 July 1497, Vasco da Gama departed Portugal with a fleet of four ships. After months of navigating unfamiliar waters and overcoming numerous challenges, the expedition reached the East African coast.
On Easter Sunday, 15 April 1498, Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored off the coast of Malindi. The arrival marked a historic moment not only for Portugal but also for the wider world, as it represented a crucial step toward establishing direct maritime trade between Europe and Asia.
Malindi played a particularly important role in the success of the expedition. The town's leaders welcomed the Portuguese visitors and provided assistance that proved essential for the continuation of the voyage toward India.
texts.5:
## Why Malindi Was Important to Portuguese Explorers
During the late fifteenth century, Malindi was one of the most prosperous and influential Swahili city-states along the East African coast. Its strategic location made it an important center for trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange.
Merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, and other regions regularly visited Malindi, contributing to a vibrant cosmopolitan society connected to the wider Indian Ocean trading world.
For Portuguese explorers seeking routes to Asia, Malindi offered a safe harbor, valuable local knowledge, and opportunities to establish diplomatic relationships. The town's rulers recognized the potential benefits of engaging with the newcomers and supported their journey.
Historical accounts indicate that Vasco da Gama received assistance from experienced navigators familiar with the monsoon wind systems of the Indian Ocean. This knowledge helped guide the Portuguese fleet across the ocean toward the western coast of India.
Without the support received in Malindi, the success of the expedition might have been far less certain.
texts.6:
## The Purpose of the Vasco da Gama Pillar
During this period, Portuguese explorers commonly erected stone markers known as padrões to commemorate important voyages and assert the presence of Portugal in newly visited territories.
These monuments served several purposes. They acted as navigational markers, symbols of diplomatic relationships, records of exploration, and visible reminders of Portuguese maritime achievements.
The Vasco da Gama Pillar in Malindi was erected as part of this tradition and became one of the most enduring symbols of Portugal's age of exploration.
Its survival over more than five centuries makes it one of the most remarkable historical monuments associated with early European exploration beyond Europe itself.
texts.7:
## Architecture and Design of the Vasco da Gama Pillar
The monument is constructed from coral stone, a material widely used along the East African coast because of its availability and durability. Positioned on a promontory overlooking the sea, the pillar was carefully placed to be visible to vessels approaching the coast.
Its elevated location provides spectacular views of the Indian Ocean and helps visitors appreciate the maritime setting that shaped the history of Malindi.
Although relatively simple in appearance compared with later colonial monuments, the pillar carries immense historical significance because of its direct association with one of the most important periods of global exploration.
The site also offers excellent opportunities for photography and remains one of the most iconic attractions within Malindi.
texts.8:
## The Vasco da Gama Pillar and Global History
The arrival of Vasco da Gama in East Africa formed part of a broader process that reshaped global trade, politics, and cultural exchange. The successful establishment of a sea route linking Europe and Asia fundamentally altered patterns of commerce and international relations.
Through this connection, goods, technologies, ideas, and people moved across vast distances with increasing frequency. The Indian Ocean became an even more important arena for interaction among civilizations from Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
The Vasco da Gama Pillar serves as a tangible reminder of these transformations and provides visitors with an opportunity to reflect on how global history has been shaped by exploration, trade, and cultural exchange.
As one of the oldest surviving monuments associated with this era, the pillar occupies a unique place within the heritage of Kenya and the wider world.
texts.30:
## Maritime Heritage at Malindi Museum
The Indian Ocean has always played a central role in the history of Malindi. Maritime heritage exhibitions explore the relationship between coastal communities and the sea, highlighting activities such as navigation, fishing, shipbuilding, and long-distance trade.
The exhibits demonstrate how generations of sailors and merchants used monsoon winds to connect East Africa with destinations across the Indian Ocean. These maritime networks facilitated cultural exchange and economic development while shaping the identity of coastal settlements.
Visitors learn about traditional seafaring technologies, trade routes, and the importance of maritime resources to local communities. These insights help explain why coastal towns such as Malindi became significant centers of commerce and cultural interaction.
The maritime collections also complement the stories associated with the Vasco da Gama Pillar and Portuguese exploration, creating a broader understanding of the region's relationship with the sea.
texts.31:
## The Webb Memorial Library
One of the lesser-known but highly valuable resources associated with Malindi Museum is the Webb Memorial Library. This specialized library contains publications, reference materials, historical records, and research resources relating to the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.
The library supports researchers, students, historians, and heritage professionals seeking deeper knowledge about the region. Its collections provide access to information that may not be readily available elsewhere.
Subjects covered include archaeology, architecture, maritime history, ethnography, environmental studies, cultural heritage management, and regional history. These resources contribute to ongoing research and support educational activities associated with the museum.
For scholars interested in the Swahili Coast, the library represents an important center of knowledge and documentation.
texts.32:
## Educational Programs and Public Learning
Education is one of the core functions of Malindi Museum. Through exhibitions, guided tours, workshops, school visits, and public programs, the museum helps make history and cultural heritage accessible to diverse audiences.
Students benefit from opportunities to engage directly with historical objects and heritage sites, while teachers can use museum resources to enrich classroom learning. Visitors of all ages gain valuable insights into the cultural and historical development of the Kenyan coast.
The museum's educational mission extends beyond formal learning by encouraging public appreciation of heritage and promoting awareness of conservation issues.
By fostering curiosity and understanding, Malindi Museum contributes to preserving cultural knowledge while inspiring future generations to value and protect their heritage.
texts.33:
## Why Malindi Museum's Collections Matter
The collections preserved by Malindi Museum are important not only because they document the past but also because they help communities understand their identity and cultural heritage. They provide tangible evidence of historical experiences, achievements, and connections that continue to shape contemporary society.
Through careful conservation and interpretation, the museum ensures that these valuable resources remain available for future generations. Visitors leave with a deeper appreciation of the diverse cultures, traditions, and historical events that have contributed to the unique character of Malindi and the Kenyan coast.
As a result, Malindi Museum plays a crucial role in preserving memory, supporting education, promoting research, and strengthening cultural understanding both within Kenya and internationally.

## [PDF page 208]
The   East   African   Coast   between   Somalia   and   Mozambique   has   for   centuries   been  
inhabited  by  people  of  various  backgrounds.  Most    of  the  Bantu  speaking  groups   arrived  
in   the area between A.D. 500 and   800 having   come from the south.  By   about A.D. 1000,  
they   had   been   joined   by   Arabs   who   came   from   Asia   to   settle   along   the   coastal   areas   of  
East  Africa.  Independent  city  states  such  as  Lamu,  Mombasa,  Malindi,  Pemba,  Kilwa  and  
Zanzibar   flourished   along   the   coast.   These   Coastal   settlements   traded   in   gold,   silk,   ivory  
and   skins   with   traders  from  as  far  as  Persia,  Arabia,  Syria,  India  and   even  China.  Some  of  
the settlements grew more powerful than others.

## [PDF page 208]
The   difference   in   wealth,   and   the   resultant   competition   for   control   of   the   trade   led   to  
rivalries   and   even   wars.  For     a   long   time   Kilwa   was   the   most   important   and   most  
prosperous   settlement   on   the   coast.  However,     by   1490,   its   prosperity   had   begun   to  
decline and   was slowly giving   way to Mombasa.  Mombasa was founded about the same  
time   with   a   rival   settlement   of   Malindi,   further   north   and   prosperity   of   Mombasa  
brought fierce   rivalries between it   and   city states including Malindi, Lamu and   Pate.

Taking   advantage   of   declining   Portuguese   control,   the   Omani   Arabs   began   to   raid   the  
Portuguese   possessions   on   the   East   African   Coast,   beginning   in   1652.  By     1678,   Fort  
Jesus,   Mombasa   was   the   only   remaining   stronghold   of   Portuguese   power   on   the  
northern   part   of   the   East   African   Coast.  The     Portuguese   were   finally   expelled   from   the  
fort,   in   December   1698   by   the   Omanis   after   a   33‐  month   siege.  The     siege   is   known   in  
history  as  the  most  remarkable  event   during   the  long  Portuguese  occupation  of  the  East  
African   Coast   displaying   the   bravery   of   the   Captain   and   his   men   during   many   months   of  
bombardment,   hunger   and   plague.  Despite     repeated   attempts   to   recapture   it,   it   was  
not until 1728 that the Portuguese managed to re‐  occupy it   but only for 18   months.

## [PDF page 210]
The   defeat   of   the   Portuguese   left   the   Omani   Arabs   in   charge   of   the   coastal   settlements  
until  the  area  was  colonized  by  the  British   in   1885.  Once   under   British   rule,   the  fort  was  
used   as   a   prison   until   1958   when   it   was   declared   a   National   Park,   subsequently  
becoming a national monument   and   a museum.  It   still serves this function to date.

Name   Fort   Jesus, Mombasa  
The   Fort   owes   its   name   to   the   history   of   religious   rivalry   between   the   Christians   and  
Muslims   in   Europe.  During     the   14th   and   15th   centuries   Europe   was   devastated   by   war  
and   schism   that   divided   the   states   at   that   time.  Social   unrest   was   so   rife   that   the   Turks  
and   Arabs   took   advantage   of   the   situation   to   advance   their   religion   in   the  
Mediterranean   regions   of   Africa   and   Europe.  On   seeing   the   whole   Christianity   under  
threat,   the   King   of   Portugal   Dom   Henry   conceived   a   plan   of   action   that   would   avoid  
further   attacks from Muslims.He   therefore instituted a new military order‐ the Order of  
Christ,   to   fight   against   the   Moors   (Muslims).  Christianity   was   now   enshrined   in   the  
structure  of  the  state;  it   was  the  responsibility  of  the  Kings   to  enforce  the  Christian   faith  
upon   the   people   through   state   machinery.  When     the   Portuguese   arrived   in   Mombasa,  
they   encountered  the  Arabs  and   this  was  reminiscent  of  the  Muslim  domination  back  at

## [PDF page 208]
The   East   African   Coast   between   Somalia   and   Mozambique   has   for   centuries   been  
inhabited  by  people  of  various  backgrounds.  Most    of  the  Bantu  speaking  groups   arrived  
in   the area between A.D. 500 and   800 having   come from the south.  By   about A.D. 1000,  
they   had   been   joined   by   Arabs   who   came   from   Asia   to   settle   along   the   coastal   areas   of  
East  Africa.  Independent  city  states  such  as  Lamu,  Mombasa,  Malindi,  Pemba,  Kilwa  and  
Zanzibar   flourished   along   the   coast.   These   Coastal   settlements   traded   in   gold,   silk,   ivory  
and   skins   with   traders  from  as  far  as  Persia,  Arabia,  Syria,  India  and   even  China.  Some  of  
the settlements grew more powerful than others.

The   difference   in   wealth,   and   the   resultant   competition   for   control   of   the   trade   led   to

prosperous   settlement   on   the   coast.  However,     by   1490,   its   prosperity   had   begun   to

brought fierce   rivalries between it   and   city states including Malindi, Lamu and   Pate.

## [PDF page 210]
Taking   advantage   of   declining   Portuguese   control,   the   Omani   Arabs   began   to   raid   the  
Portuguese   possessions   on   the   East   African   Coast,   beginning   in   1652.  By     1678,   Fort  
Jesus,   Mombasa   was   the   only   remaining   stronghold   of   Portuguese   power   on   the  
northern   part   of   the   East   African   Coast.  The     Portuguese   were   finally   expelled   from   the  
fort,   in   December   1698   by   the   Omanis   after   a   33‐  month   siege.  The     siege   is   known   in  
history  as  the  most  remarkable  event   during   the  long  Portuguese  occupation  of  the  East  
African   Coast   displaying   the   bravery   of   the   Captain   and   his   men   during   many   months   of  
bombardment,   hunger   and   plague.  Despite     repeated   attempts   to   recapture   it,   it   was  
not until 1728 that the Portuguese managed to re‐  occupy it   but only for 18   months.
texts.285:
## [PDF page 210]
The   defeat   of   the   Portuguese   left   the   Omani   Arabs   in   charge   of   the   coastal   settlements  
until  the  area  was  colonized  by  the  British   in   1885.  Once   under   British   rule,   the  fort  was  
used   as   a   prison   until   1958   when   it   was   declared   a   National   Park,   subsequently  
becoming a national monument   and   a museum.  It   still serves this function to date.
texts.286:
## [PDF page 210]
Name   Fort   Jesus, Mombasa  
The   Fort   owes   its   name   to   the   history   of   religious   rivalry   between   the   Christians   and  
Muslims   in   Europe.  During     the   14th   and   15th   centuries   Europe   was   devastated   by   war  
and   schism   that   divided   the   states   at   that   time.  Social   unrest   was   so   rife   that   the   Turks  
and   Arabs   took   advantage   of   the   situation   to   advance   their   religion   in   the  
Mediterranean   regions   of   Africa   and   Europe.  On   seeing   the   whole   Christianity   under  
threat,   the   King   of   Portugal   Dom   Henry   conceived   a   plan   of   action   that   would   avoid  
further   attacks from Muslims.He   therefore instituted a new military order‐ the Order of  
Christ,   to   fight   against   the   Moors   (Muslims).  Christianity   was   now   enshrined   in   the  
structure  of  the  state;  it   was  the  responsibility  of  the  Kings   to  enforce  the  Christian   faith  
upon   the   people   through   state   machinery.  When     the   Portuguese   arrived   in   Mombasa,  
they   encountered  the  Arabs  and   this  was  reminiscent  of  the  Muslim  domination  back  at

“Vasco da Gama’s Pillar”, now to be seen at Malindi, close to the town (to the left of it as seen from the sea) and at the extremity of a narrow rocky promontory of only a few feet in height, is certainly not the padrão erected by the great navigator, though it probably occupies its site. When Cabral arrived at Malindi in 1501 the pillar had been removed, it having proved a “stone of offence” to the people of Mombaça. The king, however, had stowed it away carefully, and had even caused the royal arms to be repainted. João de Sá, who had been with Gama, identified it.

The existing pillar, of which we give an illustration, is built up of concrete made of coral rock and lime. It rises to a height of 16 feet, and is surmounted by a cross, bearing on the sea side the arms of Portugal, but no inscription. It is not the pillar put up at the request of Vasco da Gama, but Sir John Kirk feels sure that the cross is very ancient. The latter is of sandstone, and evidently of local make, whilst the other crosses discovered hitherto are of limestone or marble. See Introduction.

When the church was desecrated in 1840, the figure was removed to another church, where Texeira de Aragão discovered it in 1853. It is now in the church at Belem. The existing pillar, of which we give an illustration, is built up of concrete made of coral rock and lime. It is not the pillar put up at the request of Vasco da Gama, but Sir John Kirk feels sure that the cross is very ancient. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
**Malindi Museum Heritage Complex**  
 [Wikimedia | © OpenStreetMap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#/map/0 "Show in full screen")  
Established May 10, 2004;22 years ago  
Coordinates3°12′57″S 40°07′19″E / 3.215922°S 40.121813°E  
Visitors 20,990 (2014)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-1)  
OwnerNational Museums of Kenya
**Malindi Museum** is a museum located in Malindi, Kenya. It has control over four main heritage sites: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and The Heritage Complex museum.

In 1991 the Malindi Museum Society was formed to support the policy of the National Museums of Kenya to acquire a historic building in Malindi that could be turned into a museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-2) Malindi's first museum building was opened in 2004, located in a two story building dating from 1891 known as The House of Columns. The building was constructed by Adulhussein Gulamhussein.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-3) The Bohra community sold the building for 2,000 English pounds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4) The building operated as an Indian trading center since its establishment in 1891.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) The building that houses the museum was used as Malindi's first native hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-6) On the east facade there is a colonnade featuring five round pillars. The building served as a hospital and headquarters of the Department of Fisheries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-7) In 1991, it was declared a national monument.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-8) In 1999 the House of Columns was transferred to the National Museum of Kenya and a restoration opened in 2004 as museum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9)

In 2013 Malindi Museum acquired a second set of buildings: the former offices of the District Commissioner, about 300 metres northwest along Silversand Road. This is now known as Malindi Museum Heritage Complex, the main building of which houses the ethnographic collections.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-10) Malindi Museum also has responsibility for two other heritage sites in the town: The Vasco da Gama Pillar and The Portuguese Chapel.
Coelacanth in The House of Columns
The Heritage Complex museum contains various historical artefacts from Malindi.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-11) The museum has exhibits containing traditional objects such as musical instruments, tools and costumes. On the ethnographic section, the museum contains various artefacts of the Mijikenda peoples who are ethnic groups inhabiting the Kenyan coast, including wooden totems,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) as well as ancient artifacts that belonged to Arabs who settled in Malindi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-12) In addition, the museum features artefacts from other communities that inhabit the Kenyan coast, as well as objects from the Swahili civilization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-13) The museum features exhibits about fish species and the history of Malindi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-14)

The House of Columns features temporary exhibits including famous _Malindi Coelacanth_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9) The museum also contains artifacts related to the explorer Vasco da Gama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-15)The House of Columns has exhibits from the Portuguese period of Kenya's coastal zone, as well as photographs of some of the country's archeological sites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-16) In addition, the museum owns the Webb Memorial Library which has books on the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-17)
A single ticket currently (2023) covers the four sites under the control of Malindi Museum. These are: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and the Malindi Museum Heritage Complex.

**The Vasco Da Gama Pillar**
The 15th Century was an era of worldwide exploration by Portugal. Early in the Century, Portugal had conceived an idea of commemorating visits of Portuguese vessels in different domains. In 1497, King Dom Manuel of Portugal appointed Vasco da Gama to command a fleet of 4 ships to sail to India through the Far East. The Fleet left Portugal on the 8th of July, 1497 and after many adventures, anchored off Malindi on Easter Sunday 15th April, 1498. Read More…
**The Portuguese Chapel**
The Portuguese presence in Malindi began with the arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498. On his second voyage to India, he left a group of solders in Malindi and a Chapel built in the style of that of the Navigator`s at Sagres in Portugal and a Portuguese` factory ‘or trading base which included store houses, barracks, residences and offices. Read More..
**The House of Columns (Malindi Museum)**
Though the date of construction of this unique structure is not known, it is known that it was used by Adulhussein Gulamhussein & Co. There is photographic evidence of its existence in 1891 when W. Fitzgerald took a picture of it from on board the IBEA’s coasting steamer, the Henry Wright, the boat that took him up to the coast from Mombasa to Lamu during his survey of the agricultural potential of the Kenya Coast. Read More..
**The Malindi Heritage Complex Museum**
This building was constructed in early 1890`s for the Imperial British East Africa Company ( IBEA Co.) which by British Royal Charter took over for 50 years the Sultan of Zanzibar`s mainland concession from Kipini to Vanga ( the coastal strip ). Mr. Bell Smith, an employee of IBEA Co., oversaw the construction of the building, known then as the District Collector`s Office, to serve as the company’s first office. Read More..

On the ethnographic section, the museum contains various artefacts of the Mijikenda peoples who are ethnic groups inhabiting the Kenyan coast, including wooden totems,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) as well as ancient artifacts that belonged to Arabs who settled in Malindi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-12) In addition, the museum features artefacts from other communities that inhabit the Kenyan coast, as well as objects from the Swahili civilization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-13) The museum features exhibits about fish species and the history of Malindi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-14)
texts.3:
The House of Columns features temporary exhibits including famous _Malindi Coelacanth_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9) The museum also contains artifacts related to the explorer Vasco da Gama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-15)The House of Columns has exhibits from the Portuguese period of Kenya's coastal zone, as well as photographs of some of the country's archeological sites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-16) In addition, the museum owns the Webb Memorial Library which has books on the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-17)
A single ticket currently (2023) covers the four sites under the control of Malindi Museum. These are: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and the Malindi Museum Heritage Complex.

**The Vasco Da Gama Pillar**
The 15th Century was an era of worldwide exploration by Portugal. Early in the Century, Portugal had conceived an idea of commemorating visits of Portuguese vessels in different domains. In 1497, King Dom Manuel of Portugal appointed Vasco da Gama to command a fleet of 4 ships to sail to India through the Far East. The Fleet left Portugal on the 8th of July, 1497 and after many adventures, anchored off Malindi on Easter Sunday 15th April, 1498. Read More…
**The Portuguese Chapel**
The Portuguese presence in Malindi began with the arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498. On his second voyage to India, he left a group of solders in Malindi and a Chapel built in the style of that of the Navigator`s at Sagres in Portugal and a Portuguese` factory ‘or trading base which included store houses, barracks, residences and offices. Read More..
**The House of Columns (Malindi Museum)**
Though the date of construction of this unique structure is not known, it is known that it was used by Adulhussein Gulamhussein & Co. There is photographic evidence of its existence in 1891 when W. Fitzgerald took a picture of it from on board the IBEA’s coasting steamer, the Henry Wright, the boat that took him up to the coast from Mombasa to Lamu during his survey of the agricultural potential of the Kenya Coast. Read More..
**The Malindi Heritage Complex Museum**
This building was constructed in early 1890`s for the Imperial British East Africa Company ( IBEA Co.) which by British Royal Charter took over for 50 years the Sultan of Zanzibar`s mainland concession from Kipini to Vanga ( the coastal strip ). Mr. Bell Smith, an employee of IBEA Co., oversaw the construction of the building, known then as the District Collector`s Office, to serve as the company’s first office. Read More..

# Magellan's Cross Tours
## Visit Magellan's Cross
#### The first Catholic Filipinos were baptized on the site of this historic chapel, believed to contain the original cross planted by Ferdinand Magellan in 1521.
Visit the ornate Spanish pavilion that shelters the holy relic of Magellan’s Cross in Cebu City. Established by Spanish and Portuguese explorers on the orders of the famous voyager Ferdinand Magellan, the cross marks the beginning of the Philippines’ Catholicization and is an important religious and historic landmark in the city. Admire the chapel’s pretty architecture and see the centuries-old cross against a backdrop of painted scenes on the ceiling.
Walk across the paved square from the Basilica Minore del Santo Niño to reach the octagonal stone chapel, which was built in 1834 to protect the holy relic. The chapel has large arched doorways and a red-tiled roof. Make your way through one of the arches and gaze up at the fabled cross. Locals say that Catholicism in the Philippines began on this very site with the baptism of King Humabon and Queen Juana. Check out the paintings on the chapel’s ceiling, which depict the stories of Magellan reaching Cebu Island’s shores, planting a cross and baptizing the Filipino chieftain.
Read the small plaque beneath the cross explaining that the original crucifix has been encased in tindalo timber to protect it from the elements. Some believe the original cross was damaged by devotees who wished to chip off pieces of wood to keep as souvenirs or miraculous relics. Others say the original cross was destroyed or stolen shortly after Magellan’s death and was quickly replaced by the replica you see today.
Although no one can say which of these stories is true, Magellan’s Cross is a wonderful place to enjoy the atmosphere of a significant pilgrimage site. Take part in the local tradition of placing a coin or a small prayer candle at the base of the cross.
Magellan’s Cross is located in historic Santo Niño, about a 25-minute walk from the Cebu-Mactan Ferry Terminal. Reach the area easily by bus to nearby Cebu City Hall. The chapel is free to visit. It is within a short walking distance from some of Cebu’s most significant historic sites, including Fort San Pedro and the Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral.

Title: Magellan’s Cross and Fort San Pedro – Pinay Travel Junkie
Chunks: 0,1
“You have not seen Magellan’s Cross?!”, a recurring question that’s been thrown at me by a handful of people. When they ask, they cast me this look of disbelief as if I’ve committed some crime.
It’s not like I’ve been to Cebu a gazillion times. Just a couple. And on my third visit, with half a day to spare, I thought it’s about time to do that mandatory photo session by the cross.
Magellan’s Cross, one of the most photographed crucifixes in the country.
I also assumed my friend Xhy and my sister Gabe, both Cebu first timers, would love to see it. Since I was sort of in charge of the itinerary (yes I made an IT due to time constraints), I was the one who looked up options for accommodation. It was my decision to stay downtown, in a place that’s within walking distance to Magellan’s Cross.
Initially, I wanted for us to check in either Century Hotel or Hotel de Mercedes. I cannot remember which is which, but one was more expensive than I thought and the other, we mysteriously couldn’t find.
Our Cebu View Tourist Inn room. Decent and worth the bucks.  
We found Cebu View Tourist Inn the night before while walking along Sanciangko Street. Room rate ain’t bad. Our air-conditioned twin bedroom cost us about P300 each, already inclusive of the charge for an extra person (but exclusive of extra pillow, bed and towel).
Our morning begun early. At 7:00 AM, we were already out. After a quick brekkie at Pete’s Kitchen along Pelaez Street, we finally made our way to Magellan’s Cross, a mere kilometer from where we were.
On the way to the cross, we passed by Basilica Minore del Santo Niño along Osmeña Boulevard. It is a 16th century church built on the spot where a sculpture of Sto. Niño (image of the Holy Child Jesus) which dates back Magellan’s time, was found by Spanish explorers. This particular Sto. Niño is said to be miraculous. I reckon it truly is, after it survived three church fires.

Flocks of pilgrims, tourists and locals shuffled to and fro. I was getting nauseous with the chaos and heat. Reason why I did not attempt to enter the church anymore. The two did not express any interest in doing so either so we moved on.
The human traffic we followed led us to Magellan’s Cross, in front of the city hall, just a few meters away from the church. The cross is a replica, and locals claim that it houses the remains of the original one.
After quick snapshots, we left the structure. The sun was glaring at 10:00 AM but I insisted we walk to nearby Fort San Pedro instead of taking a cab to save a few pesos.
Fort’s entrance.  
Fort San Pedro or Fuerza de San Pedro, the smallest and oldest fort in the country, used to be a military defense structure built in 1565 under the supervision of Miguel Lopez de Legazpi. It’s located near Pier 1, along S. Osmeña Blvd (take note of the “S.”, it’s different from the Osmeña Blvd where Basilica Minore del Santo Niño is). Admission fee P30 for adults, open from 7:00 AM to 10:00 PM.
On top of the bastion.  
The fort is now a charming walled garden. A refuge from downtown Cebu City’s bustle. Perfect time to visit at sunset when the crumbling ruin is highlighted by a faint orange glow.
Romantic spot for a stroll.  
It’s unfortunate that we didn’t have time to linger on its benches. Gabe’s flight back to Manila was that afternoon, and the rest of us will be roadtripping (and roro cruising) our way to Dumaguete after lunch.
Drained by the heat, we hailed a taxi to go back to the inn. After checking out, we’d have to bid so long to Cebu.

opened.information:
Source: http://www.anagonzales.com/2022/04/fort-san-pedro-cebu.html
Title: Fort San Pedro Cebu
Chunks: 0,1
Before my flight, I decided to check out one last tourist spot in Cebu. There are several recommendations when you search for where to go around the city, but I haven't been to Fort San Pedro so I went for it.
**Other Historical Sites Within Cebu City:**
1. Casa Gorordo Museum
2.Basilica Minore del Sto. Niño de Cebu
3.Yap-Sandiego Ancestral House
4.The Heritage of Cebu Monument
5. **Jesuit House Museum**

6. Magellan's Cross
Magellan's Cross is walking distance to the fort, so I decided to stop by prior. I've been here during my first trip in Cebu in 2013 with Paxie!Its significance is being the first Christian cross planted in the Philippines' soil.
Compared before, there were little to no people surrounding the cross. There were still candles for sale, which I had fond memories with Paxie coz we really took to heart the colors of the ones we bought. While I was there recently, you cannot go inside the pavilion.
**FORT SAN PEDRO**
I crossed the street to the Island Souvenir store, and walked further and crossed again towards a gated property which is the**Plaza Independencia** where the Fort San Pedro is located. The park is also nice and huge, but it was soooo hot when I went there so I went ahead towards the fort for shade.
Fort San Pedro, also known as the Fuerte de San Pedro, is a military defense structure built by the Spaniards to "repel Muslim raiders". It was originally made of wood, built under the command of Miguel López de Legazpi.
Meanwhile during the American regime, the barracks was converted into a school! And during the World War II, it was a place of refuge for Japanese residents, and eventually served as an emergency hospital for the wounded. If the walls could speak, Fort San Pedro hold so many stories and secrets.
There's not much to see or do during my visit in 2022, and some of the museum halls were already occupied by office spaces (??) that I was embarrassed to go in, but alam nyo naman, a little research about the place will go a long way. Knowing a bit about a structure's past and its significance to the city made the place so interesting and colorful.

- Oldest and Smallest Fort in the Philippines (2,025 sqm)

- At the fort's entrance, you'll see the Philippine flag, the image of the Santo Niño, and the seal of the Spanish king
-Every corner of this triangular fort holds a bastion for San Miguel (north) Ignacio de Loyola (southeast), and La Concepcion (southwest). You'll also spot a turret or watchtower on these corners
- There are 14 cannons around the fort

- Pre-pandemic, the lawn at the center of the triangular fort used to hold events like birthdays and weddings
You can also see the port area of Cebu City from the fort, a really beautiful view on such a clear day. I missed this, and will always love traveling around Cebu for its rich history.
_A. Pigafetta Street, Cebu City_
_Open daily, from 8AM to 7PM_
_Entrance fee: PHP 30 Adult, 20% Off for Students / Senior Citizens / PWDs_

Before my flight, I decided to check out one last tourist spot in Cebu. There are several recommendations when you search for where to go around the city, but I haven't been to Fort San Pedro so I went for it.
**Other Historical Sites Within Cebu City:**
1. Casa Gorordo Museum
2.Basilica Minore del Sto. Niño de Cebu
3.Yap-Sandiego Ancestral House
4.The Heritage of Cebu Monument
5. **Jesuit House Museum**

6. Magellan's Cross
Magellan's Cross is walking distance to the fort, so I decided to stop by prior. I've been here during my first trip in Cebu in 2013 with Paxie!Its significance is being the first Christian cross planted in the Philippines' soil.
Compared before, there were little to no people surrounding the cross. There were still candles for sale, which I had fond memories with Paxie coz we really took to heart the colors of the ones we bought. While I was there recently, you cannot go inside the pavilion.
**FORT SAN PEDRO**
I crossed the street to the Island Souvenir store, and walked further and crossed again towards a gated property which is the**Plaza Independencia** where the Fort San Pedro is located. The park is also nice and huge, but it was soooo hot when I went there so I went ahead towards the fort for shade.
Fort San Pedro, also known as the Fuerte de San Pedro, is a military defense structure built by the Spaniards to "repel Muslim raiders". It was originally made of wood, built under the command of Miguel López de Legazpi.
Meanwhile during the American regime, the barracks was converted into a school! And during the World War II, it was a place of refuge for Japanese residents, and eventually served as an emergency hospital for the wounded. If the walls could speak, Fort San Pedro hold so many stories and secrets.
There's not much to see or do during my visit in 2022, and some of the museum halls were already occupied by office spaces (??) that I was embarrassed to go in, but alam nyo naman, a little research about the place will go a long way. Knowing a bit about a structure's past and its significance to the city made the place so interesting and colorful.

- Oldest and Smallest Fort in the Philippines (2,025 sqm)

- At the fort's entrance, you'll see the Philippine flag, the image of the Santo Niño, and the seal of the Spanish king
-Every corner of this triangular fort holds a bastion for San Miguel (north) Ignacio de Loyola (southeast), and La Concepcion (southwest). You'll also spot a turret or watchtower on these corners
- There are 14 cannons around the fort

- Pre-pandemic, the lawn at the center of the triangular fort used to hold events like birthdays and weddings
You can also see the port area of Cebu City from the fort, a really beautiful view on such a clear day. I missed this, and will always love traveling around Cebu for its rich history.

“You have not seen Magellan’s Cross?!”, a recurring question that’s been thrown at me by a handful of people. When they ask, they cast me this look of disbelief as if I’ve committed some crime.
It’s not like I’ve been to Cebu a gazillion times. Just a couple. And on my third visit, with half a day to spare, I thought it’s about time to do that mandatory photo session by the cross.
Magellan’s Cross, one of the most photographed crucifixes in the country.
I also assumed my friend Xhy and my sister Gabe, both Cebu first timers, would love to see it. Since I was sort of in charge of the itinerary (yes I made an IT due to time constraints), I was the one who looked up options for accommodation. It was my decision to stay downtown, in a place that’s within walking distance to Magellan’s Cross.
Initially, I wanted for us to check in either Century Hotel or Hotel de Mercedes. I cannot remember which is which, but one was more expensive than I thought and the other, we mysteriously couldn’t find.
Our Cebu View Tourist Inn room. Decent and worth the bucks.  
We found Cebu View Tourist Inn the night before while walking along Sanciangko Street. Room rate ain’t bad. Our air-conditioned twin bedroom cost us about P300 each, already inclusive of the charge for an extra person (but exclusive of extra pillow, bed and towel).
Our morning begun early. At 7:00 AM, we were already out. After a quick brekkie at Pete’s Kitchen along Pelaez Street, we finally made our way to Magellan’s Cross, a mere kilometer from where we were.
On the way to the cross, we passed by Basilica Minore del Santo Niño along Osmeña Boulevard. It is a 16th century church built on the spot where a sculpture of Sto. Niño (image of the Holy Child Jesus) which dates back Magellan’s time, was found by Spanish explorers. This particular Sto. Niño is said to be miraculous. I reckon it truly is, after it survived three church fires.
texts.1:
Flocks of pilgrims, tourists and locals shuffled to and fro. I was getting nauseous with the chaos and heat. Reason why I did not attempt to enter the church anymore. The two did not express any interest in doing so either so we moved on.
The human traffic we followed led us to Magellan’s Cross, in front of the city hall, just a few meters away from the church. The cross is a replica, and locals claim that it houses the remains of the original one.
After quick snapshots, we left the structure. The sun was glaring at 10:00 AM but I insisted we walk to nearby Fort San Pedro instead of taking a cab to save a few pesos.
Fort’s entrance.  
Fort San Pedro or Fuerza de San Pedro, the smallest and oldest fort in the country, used to be a military defense structure built in 1565 under the supervision of Miguel Lopez de Legazpi. It’s located near Pier 1, along S. Osmeña Blvd (take note of the “S.”, it’s different from the Osmeña Blvd where Basilica Minore del Santo Niño is). Admission fee P30 for adults, open from 7:00 AM to 10:00 PM.
On top of the bastion.  
The fort is now a charming walled garden. A refuge from downtown Cebu City’s bustle. Perfect time to visit at sunset when the crumbling ruin is highlighted by a faint orange glow.
Romantic spot for a stroll.  
It’s unfortunate that we didn’t have time to linger on its benches. Gabe’s flight back to Manila was that afternoon, and the rest of us will be roadtripping (and roro cruising) our way to Dumaguete after lunch.
Drained by the heat, we hailed a taxi to go back to the inn. After checking out, we’d have to bid so long to Cebu.

# Magellan's Cross Tours
## Visit Magellan's Cross
#### The first Catholic Filipinos were baptized on the site of this historic chapel, believed to contain the original cross planted by Ferdinand Magellan in 1521.
Visit the ornate Spanish pavilion that shelters the holy relic of Magellan’s Cross in Cebu City. Established by Spanish and Portuguese explorers on the orders of the famous voyager Ferdinand Magellan, the cross marks the beginning of the Philippines’ Catholicization and is an important religious and historic landmark in the city. Admire the chapel’s pretty architecture and see the centuries-old cross against a backdrop of painted scenes on the ceiling.
Walk across the paved square from the Basilica Minore del Santo Niño to reach the octagonal stone chapel, which was built in 1834 to protect the holy relic. The chapel has large arched doorways and a red-tiled roof. Make your way through one of the arches and gaze up at the fabled cross. Locals say that Catholicism in the Philippines began on this very site with the baptism of King Humabon and Queen Juana. Check out the paintings on the chapel’s ceiling, which depict the stories of Magellan reaching Cebu Island’s shores, planting a cross and baptizing the Filipino chieftain.
Read the small plaque beneath the cross explaining that the original crucifix has been encased in tindalo timber to protect it from the elements. Some believe the original cross was damaged by devotees who wished to chip off pieces of wood to keep as souvenirs or miraculous relics. Others say the original cross was destroyed or stolen shortly after Magellan’s death and was quickly replaced by the replica you see today.
Although no one can say which of these stories is true, Magellan’s Cross is a wonderful place to enjoy the atmosphere of a significant pilgrimage site. Take part in the local tradition of placing a coin or a small prayer candle at the base of the cross.
Magellan’s Cross is located in historic Santo Niño, about a 25-minute walk from the Cebu-Mactan Ferry Terminal. Reach the area easily by bus to nearby Cebu City Hall. The chapel is free to visit. It is within a short walking distance from some of Cebu’s most significant historic sites, including Fort San Pedro and the Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral.
